caption: Galaxy NGC 5308 and its globular clusters, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: An edge-on galaxy appears in this Hubble image, encircled by a scattering of bright dots like bees swarming around a hive. The galaxy is NGC 5308, a lenticular galaxy in Ursa Major, the Great Bear, at a distance of just under 100 million light-years.

Lenticular galaxies fall somewhere between spirals and ellipticals. They are disc galaxies that have either used up or lost most of their gas and dust, so very few new stars are born in them, and their light comes mainly from old and ageing stars.

Those bright dots are globular clusters, tight and gravitationally bound swarms that can each hold hundreds of thousands of older stars. Together they form a delicate halo as they orbit the main body of the galaxy. Galaxies like this one are often accompanied by such a retinue.
explore: Old stars can still end violently. On 9 October 1996, one of NGC 5308's ageing stars exploded as a Type Ia supernova.
The faint, irregular smudge to the right of NGC 5308 is a separate galaxy with an unglamorous catalogue name, SDSS J134646.18+605911.9.

understand.summary: This image was taken in visible and near-infrared light with Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys, using blue and near-infrared filters. The colour assigned to each filter is not published.
understand.eye: The near-infrared light captured here is invisible to the eye, and the long exposure gathers far more light than any eye could, revealing faint clusters around the galaxy.

alt: An edge-on disc galaxy surrounded by many small bright dots on a dark background, with a dim irregular galaxy to its right.

caption: Galaxy triplet NGC 7173, NGC 7174 and NGC 7176, imaged by ESO's Very Large Telescope
story: Three galaxies share this frame, with NGC 7173 at the top, NGC 7174 at the bottom right and NGC 7176 at the bottom left. To some eyes, the combined shape of the lower pair resembles a sleeping baby. The trio lies about 106 million light-years away, in the direction of Piscis Austrinus, the Southern Fish, and belongs to one of the tight galaxy gatherings known as Hickson Compact Groups.

NGC 7173 and NGC 7176 are elliptical galaxies, smooth collections of stars without spiral arms. NGC 7174, by contrast, is a spiral. Its dust lanes look badly disturbed, and it trails a long, twisted tail.

That disturbance seems to show that the two lower galaxies are interacting right now, their gravity pulling each other out of shape. Astronomers have suggested that all three galaxies will eventually merge into one.
explore: The image covers an area of sky about 5.3 arcminutes across. It was assembled from data taken with the FORS1 instrument on ESO's Very Large Telescope, pulled from the ESO Science Archive, then processed by ESO's Henri Boffin.

understand.summary: This is a visible-light image made with the FORS1 instrument on ESO's Very Large Telescope through three filters, B, V and R. The colour assigned to each filter is not published.
understand.eye: The long telescope exposure collects far more light than the eye, helping to bring out faint features such as the twisted tail and dust lanes.

alt: Three galaxies against a dark sky, one at the top and two at the bottom, one of them with a long twisted tail.

caption: Dwarf galaxy IC 1613, imaged by ESO's VLT Survey Telescope
story: This image from ESO's VLT Survey Telescope in Chile shows IC 1613, a small dwarf galaxy in the constellation of Cetus. It was captured with OmegaCAM, the telescope's camera, and what makes this galaxy notable is how clean it is.

Most galaxies are laced with dust, fine grains that absorb and scatter starlight and hide much of what lies behind them. IC 1613 contains very little of this dust. That lack of dust gives astronomers an unusually clear view into the galaxy and everything it contains.

Dwarf galaxies are far smaller and fainter than big spirals like our own Milky Way, but they are common, so an unobscured one is valuable to study. With so little dust in the way, astronomers can explore the contents of IC 1613 without the usual veil dimming and reddening the light from its stars.

understand.summary: This is a visible-light image made with the OmegaCAM camera on ESO's VLT Survey Telescope, using u, g and r filters plus a hydrogen-alpha filter. The colour assigned to each filter is not published.
understand.eye: The camera's long exposures gather far more light than the eye, bringing out faint detail in the galaxy.

alt: A telescope view of the small dwarf galaxy IC 1613.

caption: Barred spiral galaxy NGC 1398, imaged by ESO's Very Large Telescope
story: Ribbons of gas and dust wrap around a pearly centre in this view of the barred spiral galaxy NGC 1398. Dark lanes of dust mottle its spiral arms, and pink-hued star-forming regions are scattered through its outer parts. The galaxy lies about 65 million light-years away in the constellation of Fornax, the Furnace.

Its arms do not begin at the very centre and swirl outward. Instead they stem from a straight bar of stars that cuts across the galaxy's middle. Around two thirds of spiral galaxies are seen to have such a bar, yet astronomers still aren't sure whether, or how, bars shape the way a galaxy behaves and develops.
The data come from FORS2, an instrument on ESO's Very Large Telescope at Paranal Observatory in Chile, which recorded the galaxy in fine detail.
explore: The picture was made for ESO's Cosmic Gems programme, an outreach effort that photographs interesting or attractive objects using telescope time that cannot be used for science. The data still go into ESO's science archive, where astronomers can use them.

understand.summary: This is a visible-light image from the FORS2 instrument on ESO's Very Large Telescope, using B, V and R filters plus a hydrogen-alpha filter that traces glowing hydrogen. The colour assigned to each filter is not published.
understand.eye: The long exposure collects far more light than the eye can, revealing faint dust lanes and pink star-forming regions that would not be visible by eye.

alt: A barred spiral galaxy with a pale bright centre and curving arms marked by dark dust lanes and pink patches.

caption: Spiral galaxy NGC 4051, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: This Hubble image shows NGC 4051, a spiral galaxy about 45 million light-years from Earth. It has a record of stellar explosions, with supernovae going off several times in recent decades, scattered through its centre and its spiral arms.

A supernova is what happens when a massive star dies at the end of its short life. The blast is so energetic and luminous that it looks like an especially bright new star, which then slowly fades. That brilliance means telescopes such as Hubble can pick supernovae out even in distant galaxies.

The three that NGC 4051 is known to have hosted are SN 1983I, SN 2003ie and SN 2010br. The first and last were type Ic supernovae, produced when the core of a massive star collapses after the star has already shed its outer hydrogen and helium, through winds or by passing material to a companion star.
explore: Because they have lost their outer layers, type Ic and type Ib supernovae are sometimes called stripped core-collapse supernovae.
NGC 4051 sits in the southern part of the Ursa Major I Cluster, a group rich in spiral galaxies that forms part of the larger Virgo Supercluster, which also contains the Milky Way.

understand.summary: This image comes from Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3, using filters from the ultraviolet through visible light. The colour assigned to each filter is not published.
understand.eye: Part of the light recorded here is ultraviolet, which the human eye cannot see, and the long exposure collects far more light than an eye could.

alt: A spiral galaxy, seen by Hubble.

caption: The Hockey Stick Galaxy, NGC 4656, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: This Hubble picture zooms in on the bright central region of NGC 4656, a galaxy found in Canes Venatici, the Hunting Dogs. From this partial view you would never guess that it is nicknamed the Hockey Stick Galaxy.

Seen in full, the galaxy is stretched into a long, warped stick that curls around at one end, rather like the blade of a hockey stick. This framing captures only the middle, so the curl lies outside the picture.

The odd shape is thought to come from interactions with a couple of close neighbours, the Whale Galaxy, NGC 4631, and a small elliptical called NGC 4627. When galaxies pass near each other, gravity can pull their gas, stars and dust into distorted new arrangements, completely reshaping them. Hubble has photographed many such interacting systems over the years.
explore: Other interacting galaxies Hubble has captured include Arp 273, which resembles a rose, and Arp 142, whose pair looks like an egg next to a penguin.

understand.summary: This image comes from Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3, using filters from the ultraviolet through visible light to near-infrared, including a hydrogen-alpha filter. The colour assigned to each filter is not published.
understand.eye: Some of the light captured, in the ultraviolet and near-infrared, is invisible to the eye, and the long exposures gather far more light than an eye could.

alt: A close view of the bright central region of an elongated galaxy.

caption: Central region of the starburst galaxy NGC 1313, imaged by ESO's Very Large Telescope
story: Green clouds and many knots of star formation crowd this view of the central parts of NGC 1313, a starburst galaxy. Its busy state is obvious at a glance, with star-forming regions everywhere.

A starburst galaxy is one making new stars at an unusually high rate. In NGC 1313, successive waves of star birth have blown and sculpted cocoons of gas called supershell nebulae, and the galaxy's centre holds a great many of them. The green patches mark gas glowing in the light of ionised oxygen, and they may hold clusters of very hot stars whose radiation makes the gas shine.

The picture was built from observations made using FORS1, an instrument mounted on one of the 8.2-metre Unit Telescopes of ESO's Very Large Telescope at Cerro Paranal. Combining broad colour filters with narrow ones tuned to single glowing gases lets astronomers map where the energetic young stars are reshaping their surroundings.
explore: The data were obtained on the night of 16 December 2003, through broad-band R, B and z filters and narrow-band filters including hydrogen-alpha and oxygen lines.

understand.summary: This colour composite was made with the FORS1 instrument on ESO's Very Large Telescope, combining broad-band visible and near-infrared filters with narrow-band filters for hydrogen and oxygen. The caption notes that green marks ionised oxygen, but the other colours' mapping is not published.
understand.eye: Narrow-band filters isolate light from single elements, and the long exposures gather far more light than the eye, so the glowing gas stands out much more than it would to an observer.

alt: The crowded centre of a galaxy with many bright star-forming knots and green glowing clouds of gas.

caption: Spiral galaxy NGC 6814, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: A brilliant nucleus sits at the heart of this face-on spiral galaxy, its sweeping arms rippled with intricate dark dust patterns and sprinkled with blue stars. This is NGC 6814, photographed by Hubble. Spiral and irregular galaxies together make up about 60% of the galaxies in the local Universe, yet like snowflakes no two spirals are alike.

That very bright nucleus is a telltale sign that NGC 6814 is a Seyfert galaxy, a type with an active centre that can emit strong bursts of radiation. Its core is a highly variable source of X-rays, which leads scientists to suspect a supermassive black hole there, weighing in at about 18 million times the mass of the Sun.
Along the spiral arms lie many regions of ionised gas. A recent burst of star birth in these big clouds has forged the brilliant blue stars seen dotted across the galaxy.

understand.summary: This image comes from Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3, using visible and near-infrared filters. The colour assigned to each filter is not published.
understand.eye: The near-infrared light included here is invisible to the eye, and the long exposure reveals fine dust detail far beyond what an eye could see.

alt: A face-on spiral galaxy with a very bright centre and sweeping arms streaked with dark dust and dotted with blue stars.

caption: Hickson Compact Group 31, imaged by the Hubble, Spitzer and GALEX space telescopes
captureDate: Hubble data: 8 August 2006; Spitzer: 22 February 2005; GALEX: 27 December 2004
story: A bright, distorted object sits left of centre in this composite, with a cigar-shaped galaxy above it, a bridge of star clusters linking them, and a long rope of bright clusters leading to another galaxy at lower right. The bright object in the middle is simply a foreground star. These are members of Hickson Compact Group 31, four dwarf galaxies about 166 million light-years away.

The distorted object is actually two dwarf galaxies colliding head-on. Myriad star clusters have formed in the debris pulled from them and at the site of the crash, and the massive, hot young stars are pouring out ultraviolet radiation that heats nearby gas clouds and makes them glow.
Encounters like this between dwarf galaxies are usually seen billions of light-years away, and so billions of years in the past. This group is unusually close, offering a nearer look at the process.
explore: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys resolved the youngest and brightest clusters, letting astronomers estimate their ages. The brightest, hefty groups of at least 100,000 stars apiece, are under 10 million years old.
The galaxies appear to be entering the final stages of assembly, and astronomers expect them to become one large elliptical galaxy in another billion years.

understand.summary: This composite combines visible and near-infrared light from Hubble's ACS and WFPC2 cameras, infrared from NASA's Spitzer Space Telescope, and ultraviolet from GALEX. The colour assigned to each dataset is not published.
understand.eye: Much of the light combined here, in the ultraviolet and infrared, is invisible to the human eye.

alt: A group of distorted galaxies linked by chains of bright star clusters, with a bright foreground star in the middle.

caption: Spiral galaxy NGC 3147, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: This Hubble image shows the spiral galaxy NGC 3147, seen from an angle that lays its shape and structure out plainly. The galaxy lies in Draco, the Dragon, and by the standards of galaxies it is a relatively close neighbour, at a distance of roughly 130 million light-years.

A spiral galaxy is a flat, rotating disc of stars, gas and dust, with arms that wind outward from a brighter central bulge. Seeing a spiral from a favourable perspective lets astronomers trace how those arms are arranged and how the disc is built.

Hubble recorded this galaxy with its Wide Field Camera 3, through filters spanning visible light and the near-infrared. Using several filters like this helps astronomers separate the light of different kinds of stars and pick out dust, which dims and reddens starlight passing through it.

understand.summary: This image comes from Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3, using filters from visible light into the near-infrared. The colour assigned to each filter is not published.
understand.eye: Part of the light recorded is near-infrared, invisible to the eye, and the long exposure gathers far more light than an eye could.

scaleExtra: NGC 3147 lies roughly 130 million light-years away, according to ESA/Hubble.
alt: A spiral galaxy seen at an angle that shows its disc and spiral structure.

caption: Galaxy cluster RX J2129, imaged by the James Webb Space Telescope
story: Mostly reddish stars and galaxies are scattered across a dark background. In the upper right, a large elliptical galaxy with a bright centre and a diffuse white glow sits among many smaller, similar galaxies, and around it are distorted images and arcs of light. This is the massive galaxy cluster RX J2129, photographed by Webb.

The cluster is heavy enough to bend space around it, so it acts like a vast lens for light passing through from behind. The concentric arcs are background objects stretched by this gravitational lensing. The effect is so strong that the picture contains three separate images of one distant galaxy, which hosts a supernova.

Hubble spotted that supernova first, and astronomers suspected it was a very distant Type Ia. Such explosions shine with a fairly consistent brightness, so how dim one appears reveals its distance, making them useful 'standard candles'.
explore: Because the supernova's true brightness is roughly known, it can also show how strongly RX J2129 magnifies things behind it, and so how massive the cluster is. In effect, it measures the lens's 'prescription'.
Webb's NIRCam measured the supernova's brightness, and NIRSpec took its spectrum, so it can be compared with Type Ia supernovae in the nearby Universe to check a trusted distance method.

understand.summary: This infrared image was taken with Webb's Near-InfraRed Camera (NIRCam). Light at 1.15 and 1.5 microns is shown in blue, 2.0 and 2.77 microns in green, and 3.56 and 4.44 microns in red.
understand.eye: All of this light is infrared, invisible to the human eye, so the colours are a translation of wavelengths we cannot see.

scaleExtra: The lensing cluster RX J2129 lies around 3.2 billion light-years from Earth, according to ESA/Webb.
alt: Reddish galaxies on a dark background, with a large bright elliptical galaxy in the upper right surrounded by smaller galaxies and curved arcs of light.

caption: Barred spiral galaxy NGC 4618, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: This Hubble image shows NGC 4618, a barred spiral galaxy with only one arm winding around its centre. That single arm sets it apart from other spirals.

The galaxy lies about 21 million light-years away in Canes Venatici and measures roughly a third of the Milky Way's diameter. It has a neighbour, NGC 4625, and the two form an interacting pair, close enough that each tugs on the other through gravity. Encounters like this may eventually lead galaxies to merge into something new, such as a ring galaxy.

NGC 4618 has a long history in astronomy. Wilhelm Herschel, the German-British astronomer who also found Uranus, discovered it in 1787. A year earlier he had argued that the fuzzy patches astronomers saw were probably big star clusters lying far beyond the individual stars he could make out.
explore: Herschel logged NGC 4618 on 9 April 1787, some years after finding Uranus. Astronomers later came to understand that the 'foggy' objects he described were galaxies.

understand.summary: This image combines visible and near-infrared exposures from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys and Wide Field Camera 3. The colour assigned to each filter is not published.
understand.eye: Part of the light is near-infrared, beyond what the eye can see, and the long exposures collect far more light than an eye could.

alt: A barred spiral galaxy with a single arm winding around its centre.

caption: Galaxy cluster MACS J1149.5+2223, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: This Hubble image shows MACS J1149.5+2223, a huge cluster of galaxies. The light we see from it set out more than 5 billion years ago, so we see the cluster as it was in the distant past.

A galaxy cluster is a vast gathering of galaxies bound together by gravity, and its enormous mass warps the space around it. Light from objects far behind the cluster is bent as it passes through, a process called gravitational lensing.

In MACS J1149.5+2223 the lensing does two things. It magnifies and distorts the light of more distant galaxies, stretching them into unfamiliar shapes. And it can split the light of a single distant object along several paths, so that the same background source appears more than once. For astronomers, a lens like this acts as a natural telescope, bringing faint, far-off galaxies into view that would otherwise be too dim to study.

understand.summary: This image combines near-infrared light from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys and Wide Field Camera 3. The colour assigned to each filter is not published.
understand.eye: The filters used record near-infrared light, invisible to the eye, and the long exposures reveal galaxies far too faint to see by eye.

scaleExtra: Light from the cluster took over 5 billion years to reach us, according to ESA/Hubble.
alt: A large cluster of galaxies, with the light of more distant galaxies magnified and distorted around it.

caption: Galaxies MCG+01-38-004 and MCG+01-38-005, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Two galaxies appear in this Hubble image, one above the other. The upper, red-tinted one is MCG+01-38-004. The lower, blue-tinted one is MCG+01-38-005, and it hides an unusual power source at its heart.

The lower galaxy has an active galactic nucleus, an especially bright and intense centre thought to be driven by a supermassive black hole that drags in surrounding material and throws out jets and radiation. That energy pours into nearby clouds of water. The hydrogen and oxygen atoms in the water absorb some of it and give it back at particular wavelengths, one of them in the microwave range. That makes MCG+01-38-005 a water megamaser, a far stronger cousin of the microwave lasers called masers.
Objects like this are useful tools. Astronomers used its microwave emission to refine the Hubble constant, which describes how fast the Universe is expanding.
explore: Microwaves are the same kind of radiation used to heat food. Across the Universe, objects give off light across the whole spectrum, from high-energy gamma rays to low-energy microwaves and radio waves.
The Hubble constant is named after Edwin Hubble, whose observations revealed that the Universe is expanding and after whom the space telescope is named.

understand.summary: This image was taken with Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 in near-ultraviolet, visible and near-infrared filters. The colour assigned to each filter is not published.
understand.eye: The microwave glow that makes the lower galaxy special does not appear in this picture. Hubble recorded ultraviolet, visible and near-infrared light, some of it beyond what the eye can see.

alt: Two galaxies, one above the other, the upper one red-tinted and the lower one blue-tinted.

caption: Spiral galaxy Messier 96, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Glowing gas swirls through this Hubble view of Messier 96 like a giant maelstrom, rippled with dark dust that spirals in towards the nucleus. The spiral galaxy lies just over 35 million light-years away in Leo, the Lion, and is roughly as massive and as large as our own Milky Way.

On closer inspection Messier 96 is lopsided. Its gas and dust are spread unevenly through weak spiral arms, the arms themselves are asymmetrical, and even its core is slightly off the galaxy's centre. Astronomers think its lopsided arms were shaped by the gravity of other galaxies in its group.

That group, the M96 Group, also contains the bright galaxies Messier 105 and Messier 95, along with a number of smaller, fainter members. It is the nearest group to contain bright spirals as well as a bright elliptical, which is Messier 105.
explore: Pierre Méchain discovered the galaxy in 1781, and Charles Messier added it to his famous catalogue of astronomical objects only four days later.

understand.summary: This image comes from Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3, using blue, green and near-infrared filters. The colour assigned to each filter is not published.
understand.eye: Part of the light is near-infrared, beyond human vision, and the long exposure gathers far more light than an eye could.

alt: A spiral galaxy of glowing gas streaked with dark dust swirling in towards its nucleus.

caption: Markarian 779 and neighbouring galaxies, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Several galaxies share this Hubble frame. At the bottom, a tilted spiral glows behind a star of our own Milky Way. A small spiral sits at the top centre, and at the very top is Markarian 779, a galaxy with a distorted, peculiar shape.

Markarian 779 probably looks this way because two spiral galaxies recently merged. The collision destroyed their spiral arms and scattered much of their gas and dust, leaving a single galaxy of unusual form.

It takes its name from a catalogue of more than 1500 galaxies compiled by the Armenian astronomer B. E. Markarian, who studied them in the 1960s. He searched the sky for bright objects giving off unusually strong ultraviolet light. That light can come from an active nucleus powered by a supermassive black hole, or from starbursts, intense episodes of star formation possibly set off by collisions. So Markarian galaxies are often studied to understand active galaxies, starbursts and mergers.
explore: Because ultraviolet light has several possible sources, the objects in the Markarian catalogue are quite varied.

understand.summary: The caption says this image was taken with Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3. The filters used and the colour mapping are not published.
understand.eye: The long exposure collects far more light than the eye, so faint galaxies appear clearly.

alt: Several galaxies, with a tilted spiral at the bottom behind a foreground star, a small spiral at top centre and a distorted galaxy at the top.

caption: Spiral galaxy IC 5052, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Speckled with blue, white and yellow light, this Hubble image shows part of the spiral galaxy IC 5052, seen side-on and surrounded by distant stars and galaxies. Its blue-white glow picks out a narrow, intricate structure. The galaxy lies in Pavo, the Peacock, in the southern sky.

From this edge-on angle it is hard to work out how a spiral is arranged. IC 5052 is in fact a barred spiral, with arms that do not start at the very centre but attach to the ends of a straight bar of stars crossing its middle. Roughly two thirds of spirals, the Milky Way among them, have such a bar.

Pale blue bursts along the galaxy's length, partly hidden by winding lanes of darker gas and dust, are pockets of extremely hot newborn stars. Bars are thought to aid their formation by funnelling material inward from the arms towards these stellar nurseries.
explore: Contestant Serge Meunier entered a version of this picture in Hubble's Hidden Treasures image processing competition.

understand.eye: The near-infrared light included is invisible to the eye, and the long exposure brings out faint background galaxies no eye could see.

alt: A narrow, edge-on spiral galaxy speckled with blue, white and yellow light and crossed by dark dust lanes, among distant stars and galaxies.

caption: Spiral galaxy NGC 3344, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: We see the spiral galaxy NGC 3344 face-on in this Hubble image, which makes its structure easy to study. An outer ring swirls around an inner ring, with a subtle bar of stars across the centre. The galaxy is around half the size of the Milky Way and lies 25 million light-years away.

Young stars dominate its central regions, and its outer edges also host areas of active star formation. Central bars appear in around two thirds of spiral galaxies, and the one in NGC 3344 is clearly visible, though less pronounced than some.

The galaxy holds a puzzle. The crowded stars near a galaxy's centre exert enough gravity to steer other stars, yet NGC 3344's outer stars move in an unusual way that the bar cannot fully explain. One possibility is that it once passed close to another galaxy and captured some of its stars, but more research is needed before anyone can say so confidently.
explore: The picture combines visible and near-infrared exposures from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys. The view spans around 3.4 arcminutes on each side, roughly a tenth of the full Moon's diameter.

understand.summary: This image combines visible and near-infrared light captured by Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys. The colour assigned to each filter is not published.
understand.eye: The near-infrared light included is invisible to the human eye, and the long exposures reveal detail far beyond what the eye could pick out.

alt: A face-on spiral galaxy with an inner and outer ring around a faint central bar.

caption: Stars in the heart of spiral galaxy NGC 300, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Countless stars fill this Hubble image of the heart of NGC 300, each resolved as its own point of light like grains of sand on a beach. Hot, young blue stars cluster in the spiral arms, ribbons of deep red trace curtains of dust that partly hide the stars behind, and near the centre lies the galaxy's bright, compact nucleus.

NGC 300 is a spiral much like the Milky Way and one of its closer neighbours, 6.5 million light-years away in the Sculptor group. From the ground only its brightest stars can be singled out, but Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys, with resolution some 10 times sharper, separates many more. Even so, the packed nucleus defeats it.

These data are testing a new way to measure distances to galaxies, using luminous blue supergiants. By combining their brightness with temperature, surface gravity and mass outflow, astronomers hope to check it against traditional methods based on Cepheid variables.
explore: The Sculptor group of galaxies is named for the southern constellation in which it is found.
Measuring distances is a perpetual but important concern in astronomy, and Cepheids, stars that pulsate with a period linked to their brightness, have long been one of the standard tools.

understand.summary: This colour composite was made with Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys from images taken through blue, green and near-infrared filters. The exact colour assigned to each filter is not published.
understand.eye: Part of the light is near-infrared, invisible to the eye, and no eye or ground-based telescope could separate these stars as Hubble does.

alt: A dense field of individual stars with clusters of blue stars, reddish dust ribbons and a bright compact nucleus near the centre.

caption: Edge-on spiral galaxy ESO 373-8, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: A thin, glittering streak crosses this Hubble image. It is the spiral galaxy ESO 373-8, seen edge-on some 25 million light-years away, with everything in it lined up in one flat plane. It belongs to the NGC 2997 group, along with at least seven neighbouring galaxies.

We see so many flat, pancake-like galaxies that their shape seems unremarkable. They are flattened because of a principle called conservation of angular momentum, which you can feel in a swivel chair. Spin with arms and legs out, pull them in, and you speed up.

This galaxy started as a huge, slowly rotating ball of gas. As it collapsed under its own gravity its spin quickened until, like pizza dough flung and stretched in the air, it flattened into a disc. Anything that drifted up or down out of that disc was pulled back into line, leaving the neat, streamlined shape we see today.
explore: The same rule applies at every scale. Angular momentum is conserved in a spinning galactic disc far across space just as it is for anyone twirling in an office chair.

alt: A thin, glittering edge-on galaxy stretched across the frame.

caption: Barred spiral galaxy NGC 1345, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: The loose, ragged arms of the spiral galaxy NGC 1345 fill this Hubble image, and all around it are more distant galaxies of many shapes and sizes, some even shining through the foreground galaxy. An elongated bar stretches out from its nucleus, with spiral arms reaching outward from it, which makes NGC 1345 a barred spiral.

The galaxy belongs to the Eridanus Galaxy Cluster, which gathers about 70 galaxies some 85 million light-years away in Eridanus, the River. The Fornax Cluster looks close by on the sky, though the two are really about 20 million light-years apart. Together they are called the Fornax or Southern Supercluster.

Sorting galaxies by shape tells astronomers a great deal about how the Universe has evolved, and people turn out to be better at recognising shapes than computers. That is why the citizen-science project Galaxy Zoo: Hubble has invited the public to help classify galaxies in Hubble's archive.
explore: John Herschel discovered NGC 1345 in 1835 while observing from South Africa. He called it small and very faint, and even today it shows up as only a small, round fuzz in a fairly large amateur telescope.

understand.summary: This image was made with the Wide Field Channel of Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys. Light through a blue filter (F435W) is shown in blue and light through a near-infrared filter (F814W) in red.
understand.eye: The red channel is near-infrared light, invisible to the eye, and the exposures, 17.5 minutes per filter, gather far more light than an eye could.

alt: A spiral galaxy with a central bar and loose, ragged arms, surrounded by many more distant galaxies of different shapes and sizes.

caption: Barred spiral galaxy NGC 1559, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: This Hubble view from the Wide Field Camera 3 shows NGC 1559, a barred spiral roughly 50 million light-years away in Reticulum, the Reticule, a southern constellation that astronomers rarely study. Its massive spiral arms are packed with star formation.

The galaxy holds the mass of around ten billion Suns, which sounds large but is almost 100 times less than the Milky Way. It is also receding from us at about 1300 km/s. On the sky it appears near the Large Magellanic Cloud, one of our nearest neighbours, but that is only a chance alignment. Physically, NGC 1559 is a genuine loner, with no nearby galaxies and no membership of any cluster.
For a loner, it has been busy. Astronomers have seen four supernovae, exploding stars, go off in NGC 1559, in 1984, 1986, 2005 and 2009.
explore: The four explosions are catalogued as SN 1984J, SN 1986L, SN 2005df, which was a Type Ia, and SN 2009ib, a Type II-P supernova with an unusually long plateau in its fading light.

understand.eye: Some of the light recorded lies in the ultraviolet and near-infrared, beyond what the eye can see, and the exposures collect far more light than an eye could.

alt: A barred spiral galaxy with massive spiral arms.

caption: Starburst spiral galaxy NGC 4536, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: This detailed Hubble portrait, taken with the Wide Field Camera 3, shows NGC 4536, a spiral galaxy roughly 50 million light-years away in Virgo, the Virgin. It is a starburst galaxy, a hub of extreme star formation.

How galaxies form and change over time is still far from fully understood, which is why starburst galaxies are so useful. In them, one region or many is forming stars at such a breakneck pace that the galaxy is consuming its gas faster than the supply can be topped up. Studying the conditions inside them tells astronomers a lot about how galaxies evolve.

Several things can set off such a frenzy, but every one of them needs a large enough supply of gas. A galaxy might gain it by passing very close to another galaxy, by colliding outright with one, or through some other event that squeezes a great deal of gas into a relatively small space, where it can collapse into new stars.

understand.eye: Part of the light is near-infrared, invisible to the eye, and the long exposure collects far more light than an eye could.
