caption: Blue compact dwarf galaxy PGC 51017, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: A bright streak of glowing gas and stars runs across this Hubble image. This is PGC 51017, also known as SBS 1415+437, a type of galaxy called a blue compact dwarf.

It is a well-studied galaxy with an interesting history. Astronomers first thought it was very young, going through its first burst of star formation. More recent studies suggest it is a little older, containing stars more than 1.3 billion years old.

Starbursts are short, intense bouts of star formation in which a galaxy rapidly uses up large amounts of gas making new stars. Such bursts are known in gas-rich discs and in certain low-mass dwarfs, but it is unclear whether every dwarf galaxy goes through them. Some may cycle through repeated bursts over time. Dwarfs of this kind are thought to date from the early Universe, making some of the first stars. Those with very few heavy elements, like this one, remain good places to study star formation resembling conditions in the early Universe.
explore: Heavier elements build up as generations of stars live and die, so a galaxy poor in them has seen little of that recycling. Even so, our nearby patch of the Universe may not hold any galaxy that is going through its very first burst of star formation right now.
Nick Rose entered a version of this image in Hubble's Hidden Treasures image processing competition.

understand.summary: This image was taken with Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys using visible and near-infrared filters plus a hydrogen-alpha filter that traces glowing hydrogen. The colour assigned to each filter is not published.
understand.eye: Part of the light is near-infrared, which the eye cannot see, and the long exposure gathers far more light than any eye.

alt: A bright elongated streak of glowing gas and stars.

caption: Core of the starburst galaxy NGC 1569, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: The brilliant core of NGC 1569 sparkles with light from millions of young stars in this Hubble image. At its centre are giant star clusters sitting in a large cavity, with sculpted gas structures around them and two huge gas bubbles at left, floating like islands. The thousands of tiny white dots are stars in the galaxy's halo, and the biggest and brightest objects are foreground stars in the Milky Way.

Among galaxies in our local neighbourhood, NGC 1569 is one of the most active, making stars 100 times faster than the Milky Way, at an almost continuous pace for the past 100 million years. Its central clusters each hold more than a million stars.

The cavity was blown out by massive young stars that already exploded as supernovae. Those blasts also drove a violent outflow of gas and particles that is carving giant structures, one of them, at lower right, about 3700 light-years long.
explore: The whole core is 5000 light-years wide. The largest bubble is about 378 light-years across and the smallest 119 light-years, lit by bright young stars inside them.

A new analysis puts the galaxy 11 million light-years away, farther than thought, in a group of about 10 galaxies centred on a spiral galaxy. Interactions there may be compressing its gas and sparking star birth.

understand.summary: This image combines data from Hubble's Wide Field Planetary Camera 2 and Advanced Camera for Surveys, including visible-light filters and narrow filters that isolate glowing hydrogen, nitrogen and oxygen. The colour assigned to each filter is not published.
understand.eye: Narrow-band filters isolate the glow of particular gases, and Hubble's sharp view picks out individual halo stars as tiny white dots.

alt: The bright core of a galaxy crowded with young stars, with a central cavity, sculpted gas structures, gas bubbles on the left and many tiny white dots around it.

caption: Spiral galaxy NGC 3521, imaged by ESO's Very Large Telescope
story: This picture shows NGC 3521, a large spiral galaxy in Leo, the Lion. It was taken with the FORS1 instrument on ESO's Very Large Telescope, which stands at Paranal Observatory in Chile. At only 35 million light-years away, it counts as a nearby galaxy.

A spiral galaxy like this is a vast rotating disc of stars, gas and dust, with a brighter central bulge and arms winding out from it. Our own Milky Way is a spiral too, so looking at galaxies such as NGC 3521 gives astronomers an outside view of the kind of system we live in, something we can never get of our own galaxy.

The image was built from three separate exposures, each taken through a different filter. One passed blue light, one yellow-green light and one near-infrared light. Combining them into a single colour picture lets astronomers compare how the galaxy looks at different wavelengths, since dust and stars of different ages stand out differently at each.

understand.summary: This image comes from the FORS1 instrument on ESO's Very Large Telescope. Blue light is shown as blue, yellow-green light as green and near-infrared light as red.
understand.eye: The red channel records near-infrared light, which the eye cannot see, and the long exposures gather far more light than an eye could.

alt: The large spiral galaxy NGC 3521.

caption: The Propeller Galaxy, NGC 7479, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: The tightly wound arms of the spiral galaxy NGC 7479 trace an inverted 'S' in this Hubble image, turning anticlockwise. Many bright young stars dot its arms and disc. The three brightest stars nearby, though, are foreground stars that simply lie between the galaxy and Hubble.

In radio light, the galaxy, sometimes called the Propeller Galaxy, seems to spin the other way. It has a jet of radiation that bends opposite to the stars and dust in its arms. Astronomers think a merger with another galaxy set the radio jet into this strange backwards twist.

Galactic collisions tend to reignite star formation, and NGC 7479 is indeed going through a starburst. Through a moderate-sized telescope it appears as an elongated fuzzy patch of light, while its spiral arms can be glimpsed, with more difficulty, in larger telescopes under dark skies.
explore: The image was made with the Wide Field Channel of Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys. Each filter had a total exposure of 520 seconds, and the view spans 2.7 arcminutes.

understand.summary: This image combines visible and near-infrared light from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys. Light through a yellow filter (F555W) is coloured blue and near-infrared light (F814W) is coloured red.
understand.eye: The red channel is near-infrared light, invisible to the eye, and the colours are assigned rather than natural.

alt: A spiral galaxy whose tightly wound arms form an inverted S shape, with three bright foreground stars nearby.

caption: Merging galaxies II ZW 96, imaged by the James Webb Space Telescope
story: A galaxy merger sits at the centre of this Webb image. The blue cores of two galaxies lie below centre, wrapped in red star-forming regions that stretch up through and above the middle. The lower galaxy is still a mostly regular spiral, while the upper one is heavily distorted. Faint yellow diffraction spikes appear in the middle, and many tiny background galaxies are dotted across the black sky.

Catalogued as II ZW 96, the pair lies roughly 500 million light-years away in Delphinus, near the celestial equator. Their collision has given them a chaotic shape, with bright tendrils of star formation connecting their cores and the lower galaxy's arms twisted out of shape.

Those star-forming regions make the pair very bright in infrared light, which is exactly why Webb targeted it. It is one of the Luminous Infrared Galaxies, which glow more than 100 billion times as brightly as the Sun at these wavelengths.
explore: An international team proposed studying complex galaxy systems like this soon after Webb was commissioned, to test the telescope. Their targets had already been observed with Hubble and ground-based telescopes, allowing comparison.
MIRI was contributed by ESA and NASA, built by a consortium of European institutes with JPL and the University of Arizona, which also provided NIRCam.

understand.summary: This infrared image combines Webb's NIRCam and MIRI instruments. Light at 1.5 microns is shown in blue, 2.0 microns in cyan, 3.56 and 5.6 microns in green, and 4.4, 7.7 and 15 microns in red.
understand.eye: All of this light is infrared and invisible to the eye. The colours translate wavelengths we cannot see, and the diffraction spikes come from the telescope itself.

alt: Two merging galaxies with blue cores below centre, surrounded by red star-forming regions, one galaxy distorted, on a black background with many tiny galaxies.

caption: Galaxy group HCG 86, imaged by ESO's VLT Survey Telescope
story: Four galaxies form a loose triangle in this image from ESO's VLT Survey Telescope, with three in a straight line and one below them. The bright objects just right of the elongated galaxy do not belong to the group. Together the four make up HCG 86, about 270 million light-years from Earth in Sagittarius.

HCG stands for Hickson Compact Group, a name for groups of four to ten galaxies packed very close together. That closeness makes such groups ideal places to study how galaxies interact, sometimes to the point of merging.

This view was made by a team led by Rossella Ragusa of Italy's Istituto Nazionale di Astrofisica. The survey telescope can pick up very faint structures in the outer parts of galaxies, relics of old interactions. By mapping the light in and around the group, the team concluded these faint features are remains of satellite galaxies swallowed by the group around seven billion years ago.
explore: The image is part of the VST Early-type Galaxy Survey, known as VEGAS.

The VST, at ESO's Paranal Observatory in Chile, is one of the world's largest telescopes built to survey the sky in visible light. It marked a decade of operation in 2021, helping search for exoplanets and probe our galaxy and the wider Universe.

understand.summary: This visible-light image was taken with the OmegaCAM camera on ESO's VLT Survey Telescope through g, r and i filters. The colour assigned to each filter is not published.
understand.eye: The long exposures gather far more light than the eye, which helps reveal the faint structures in the galaxies' outskirts.

alt: Four galaxies arranged in a triangle, three in a row and one below, with some bright objects to the right of the elongated galaxy.

caption: Spiral galaxy NGC 5643, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: This Hubble image shows the spiral galaxy NGC 5643 in Lupus, the Wolf, about 60 million light-years from Earth. Reaching this level of detail took thirty separate exposures, adding up to 9 hours of observing time, together with Hubble's sharp resolution.

The galaxy recently hosted a supernova, though the explosion itself is not visible. Called SN 2017cbv, it was a particular kind of explosion in which a white dwarf, the dense remnant of a star, draws so much material off a companion star that it turns unstable and blows apart. The energy released makes that region of the galaxy flare brightly.

These observations were proposed by Adam Riess, who shared the 2011 Nobel Prize in physics with Saul Perlmutter and Brian Schmidt for their part in discovering that the expansion of the Universe is accelerating.

understand.summary: This image comes from Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3, using filters from visible light into the near-infrared. The colour assigned to each filter is not published.
understand.eye: Part of the light is near-infrared, invisible to the eye, and hours of exposure gather far more light than any eye could.

alt: A spiral galaxy with detailed arms seen by Hubble.

caption: Barred spiral galaxy NGC 4700, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Bright, pinkish clouds are scattered through NGC 4700 in this Hubble image, signs that the galaxy is busy giving birth to many new stars. It is a barred spiral, similar in structure to the Milky Way, lying about 50 million light-years away in Virgo, the Virgin.

Those pink clouds are H II regions. In them, fierce ultraviolet light from hot young stars makes the nearby hydrogen gas glow. They tend to appear alongside the vast molecular clouds where fresh stars are born, and the young stars ionise the gas around them.

Astronomers study H II regions both in the Milky Way and in other galaxies where they are easy to see. They use them to gauge the chemical makeup of these environments and to learn how that shapes star formation. The first one ever recorded was the Orion Nebula, spotted through a telescope in 1610 by the French astronomer Nicolas-Claude Fabri de Peiresc.
explore: William Herschel discovered NGC 4700 in March 1786 and described it as a 'very faint nebula'. Because the Universe is expanding, the galaxy recedes from us at about 1400 km/second.

understand.summary: This image was taken with Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys through a red filter and a hydrogen-alpha filter that picks out glowing hydrogen. The colour assigned to each filter is not published.
understand.eye: The hydrogen-alpha filter isolates the glow of hydrogen gas, making star-forming clouds stand out far more than they would to the eye.

alt: A galaxy dotted with many bright pinkish clouds of glowing gas.

caption: Spiral galaxy NGC 4242, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: This Hubble image shows the bright centre of the galaxy NGC 4242, surrounded by a dimmer, more diffuse fuzz. The galaxy sits in Canes Venatici, the Hunting Dogs, a small northern constellation, some 30 million light-years away. That is not far by astronomical standards, and even a basic telescope can pick it up.

It may look fairly bright, but studies show NGC 4242 is actually quite dim, with a moderate-to-low surface brightness and low luminosity. It also forms stars at a low rate. A weak bar of stars seems to cut through its lopsided centre, and its spiral structure is very faint and poorly defined across its disc.
By most measures, then, NGC 4242 is an unexceptional galaxy, though its bright centre fading into a dimmer, more diffuse glow still makes a beautiful and ethereal sight.
explore: The British astronomer William Herschel discovered NGC 4242 in 1788.

understand.summary: This image comes from Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3, with filters ranging from the ultraviolet through visible light to the near-infrared, plus a hydrogen-alpha filter. The colour assigned to each filter is not published.
understand.eye: Some of the light captured is ultraviolet or near-infrared, invisible to the eye, and the long exposure makes this dim galaxy look brighter than it would appear to an observer.

alt: A galaxy with a bright centre surrounded by dimmer, diffuse glow.

caption: Warped barred spiral galaxy NGC 2146, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: An immense, dusty arm of glittering material lies directly across the centre of NGC 2146 in this Hubble image. The galaxy has been badly warped and stretched out of shape, and that looping arm is its most distinctive feature from our point of view.

NGC 2146 is classed as a barred spiral. Pulling one of its arms out of place and twisting it by up to 45 degrees would take colossal forces. The likeliest culprit is a neighbouring galaxy whose gravity is disturbing it and distorting the orbits of many of its stars. We are probably seeing the late stages of a process that has run for tens of millions of years.

The galaxy is also going through intense bursts of star formation, making it a starburst galaxy. That is common for barred spirals, but the extra gravitational stress here is likely making it stronger by squeezing hydrogen-rich clouds and triggering star birth.
explore: NGC 2146 is about 80 000 light-years across, a little smaller than the Milky Way, and lies about 70 million light-years away in Camelopardalis, the Giraffe. Friedrich Winnecke first spotted it in 1876 with a 16 cm telescope.

understand.summary: This image comes from the Wide Field Channel of Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys. A near-infrared filter (F814W) is shown in blue and orange-brown, a hydrogen filter (F658N) in red, and a green channel was made by combining the two.
understand.eye: Near-infrared light is invisible to the eye, and the green channel is synthesised, so these colours are an approximation of a natural view.

alt: A warped galaxy with an immense dusty arm lying across its centre.

caption: Hickson Compact Group 59, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Galaxies of very different kinds share this Hubble frame. There are two large spirals, one seen face-on with smooth arms and delicate threads of dust, the other steeply tilted. Beside them is a strangely disorderly galaxy with clumps of blue young stars, and many smaller, probably more distant galaxies fill the background.

This is Hickson Compact Group 59. The astronomer Paul Hickson catalogued unusually tight groupings of galaxies in 1982, and this was the 59th in his list. The group stands out for how varied its members are.

Hickson groups tend to be peculiar places. They often give off radio and infrared light and host active star-forming regions. Their galaxies frequently contain active galactic nuclei, bright centres powered by supermassive black holes, and large amounts of dark matter, the unseen material detected only by its gravity.
explore: The picture was made with the Wide Field Channel of Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys through blue, yellow and near-infrared filters, with total exposures of 57, 41 and 35 minutes. It covers about 3.4 arcminutes of sky.

understand.summary: This image combines blue, yellow and near-infrared filters (F435W, F606W and F814W) on Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys. The colour assigned to each filter is not published.
understand.eye: The near-infrared light is invisible to the eye, and exposures lasting most of an hour per filter reveal faint background galaxies far beyond what an eye could see.

alt: A group of galaxies, including a face-on spiral, a tilted spiral and a disorderly galaxy with blue clumps, with many small galaxies in the background.

caption: Barred spiral galaxy UGC 12158, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: The barred spiral UGC 12158 faces Hubble head-on here, its structure laid out in fine detail. Just to the lower left of the centre is a bright blue star. Unlike the several foreground stars around it, this one is a supernova inside the galaxy itself, about 400 million light-years away.

UGC 12158 is a textbook example of a barred spiral in the Hubble sequence, a scheme that sorts galaxies by shape. Its arms sweep out from a bar-shaped centre. About two thirds of spirals have bars, which are thought to funnel gas to the middle, where it piles up and forms new stars. Astronomers think bars slowly fade over time, so these galaxies eventually become regular spirals.

A galaxy's appearance barely changes over millions of years, but a supernova is brief. This one, SN 2004ef, was found in September 2004 by a pair of British amateur astronomers, and these Hubble data were part of the follow-up.
explore: The exposures were 1160, 700, 700 and 1200 seconds, and the picture spans about 2.3 arcminutes.

understand.summary: This image comes from the Wide Field Channel of Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys. Blue light (F475W) is shown in blue, yellow light (F606W) in green, and red light (F814W) plus a filter isolating glowing hydrogen in red.
understand.eye: The long exposures gather far more light than the eye, and the hydrogen filter picks out glowing gas that ordinary colour vision would not isolate.

alt: A face-on barred spiral galaxy with a bright blue point just to the lower left of its centre, and several foreground stars.

caption: Dwarf galaxy NGC 5264, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys captured the glow of distant stars in NGC 5264, a dwarf galaxy with an irregular shape and knots of blue star formation. It lies just over 15 million light-years away in Hydra, the Sea Serpent.

Dwarf galaxies like this one usually hold around a billion stars, only one per cent of the number in the Milky Way. They are generally found orbiting larger galaxies, and they are thought to form from material left over when their bigger relatives came together in a messy process.

Unlike the more common spiral and elliptical galaxies, NGC 5264 has no neat shape. Astronomers believe it was bent this way by gravitational encounters with other nearby galaxies. Those past close passes also set off new generations of star formation, and the young stars that resulted now shine in bright shades of blue across the galaxy.

understand.summary: This image combines visible and near-infrared light captured by Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys. The colour assigned to each filter is not published.
understand.eye: Part of the light is near-infrared, invisible to the eye, and the long exposure gathers far more light than an eye could.

alt: An irregularly shaped dwarf galaxy made of many faint stars, with knots of blue.

caption: Barred spiral galaxy NGC 3455, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: This Hubble image shows NGC 3455, a spiral galaxy about 65 million light-years away in Leo, the Lion. Its partner galaxy, NGC 3454, lies just outside the frame.

Astronomers sort galaxies by their structure and appearance using the Hubble Sequence, a scheme devised by Edwin Hubble. In that system NGC 3455 is a type SB galaxy, a barred spiral, meaning a bar of stars seems to slice through the central bulge. Around two thirds of spirals are barred. The SB class is then split according to how the arms look. SBa galaxies have tightly wound arms, SBc galaxies have loose ones, and SBb galaxies like NGC 3455 fall in between.
The pair belongs to the NGC 3370 group, itself one of the Leo II groups, a big scattering of galaxies lying some 30 million light-years off to the right of the Virgo cluster.
explore: Contestant Nick Rose entered a version of this image in Hubble's Hidden Treasures image processing competition.

understand.summary: This image comes from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys, combining a blue filter and a near-infrared filter. The colour assigned to each filter is not published.
understand.eye: Part of the light is near-infrared, invisible to the eye, and the long exposure collects far more light than an eye could.

alt: A barred spiral galaxy, with a bar of stars crossing its central bulge.

caption: Observed fields in spiral galaxy NGC 300, studied with ESO's Very Large Telescope
story: This picture marks the locations of three fields in NGC 300, a spiral galaxy in Sculptor, where astronomers took deep near-infrared images with the ISAAC instrument on ESO's Very Large Telescope. The observations were made through the J and K filters, two bands of infrared light.

The fields hold some special stars. Together they contain 16 Cepheids, with periods ranging from 6 to 83 days. A Cepheid is a pulsating star that brightens and dims in a regular rhythm, and the length of that rhythm is tied to how luminous the star really is.

That link makes Cepheids valuable measuring sticks. Once astronomers know a Cepheid's true brightness from its period, comparing it with how bright it appears reveals its distance. Observing them in infrared light helps too, because dust, which dims and reddens starlight, affects infrared light much less than visible light, so the measurements are cleaner.

understand.summary: The observations described used the ISAAC instrument on ESO's Very Large Telescope through near-infrared J and K filters. The colour mapping of this picture is not published.
understand.eye: The J and K bands are infrared, invisible to the eye.

alt: The spiral galaxy NGC 300 with three observed fields marked on it.

caption: 'Mystic Mountain' in the Carina Nebula, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: A craggy peak wrapped in wispy clouds rises through this Hubble image, like a scene out of a fantasy novel. It is the top of a three-light-year-tall pillar of gas and dust, and it is being eaten away by the brilliant light of nearby stars. Streamers of hot gas flow off its ridges, and veils of starlit dust float around its peaks.

The pillar sits inside the Carina Nebula, a turbulent stellar nursery 7500 light-years away. Scorching radiation and fast winds of charged particles from super-hot newborn stars are shaping and compressing it, prompting new stars to form inside. Its densest parts are resisting erosion.

It is also under attack from within. Young stars buried in the pillar fire off jets. One pair shoots out both ways from the pedestal at the top, and another from a peak near the centre. These jets, HH 901 and HH 902, are signs of star birth, launched by discs of gas and dust feeding the stars.
explore: This image was released to celebrate 20 years since Hubble was launched and placed into orbit around the Earth.

understand.summary: This image comes from Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3. Blue shows the glow of oxygen, green shows hydrogen and nitrogen, and red shows sulphur.
understand.eye: The colours isolate light from particular elements, so they map chemistry rather than the hues an eye would see.

alt: A craggy pillar of gas and dust with wispy clouds around its peaks and thin jets of gas streaming from its tips.

caption: The Orion Nebula, imaged by the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope, La Silla, Chile
story: This image of the Orion Nebula, also known as Messier 42, was made using the Wide Field Imager, a camera mounted on the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope, which stands at ESO's La Silla Observatory in Chile. It is a composite of several exposures taken through five different filters.

The Orion Nebula is a star-forming region, a cloud of gas in which new stars are being born. It is classed as an emission nebula, or H II region, made of hydrogen gas that glows because hot young stars are flooding it with energetic light. That glowing hydrogen is one of the things this image was designed to capture.

Each filter admits a different slice of light. Combining them into one picture lets astronomers show several kinds of emission at once, from the ultraviolet end of the spectrum to the red glow of hydrogen, so that different parts of the cloud and its stars stand out from one another.
explore: The exposures lasted about 52 minutes through each filter.

understand.summary: This image comes from the Wide Field Imager on the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope. Red-filter light and glowing hydrogen are shown in red, yellow-green light in green, blue light in blue and ultraviolet light in purple.
understand.eye: The ultraviolet light shown in purple is invisible to the eye, and exposures of nearly an hour per filter gather far more light than an eye could.

alt: The Orion Nebula, a large glowing cloud of gas.

caption: The Helix Nebula in infrared light, imaged by ESO's VISTA telescope
story: This unusual view of the Helix Nebula, also catalogued as NGC 7293, comes from ESO's Visible and Infrared Survey Telescope for Astronomy, known as VISTA. The Helix is a planetary nebula about 700 light-years away, and it is surrounded by a rich background of stars and galaxies.

A planetary nebula forms when a star like the Sun nears the end of its life and puffs its outer layers of gas out into space, where the hot core left behind makes them glow. Despite the name, planetary nebulae have nothing to do with planets.

VISTA observed the nebula in infrared light, and its infrared vision picks out strands of cold gas in the nebula that are mostly hidden in ordinary visible-light images of the Helix. It also reveals the many stars and galaxies in the background, giving a fuller picture of the nebula and its surroundings.

understand.summary: This colour picture was made by ESO's VISTA telescope and its VIRCAM camera from images taken through Y, J and K infrared filters. The colour assigned to each filter is not published.
understand.eye: All of this light is infrared, invisible to the eye. The strands of cold gas VISTA recorded are mostly hidden in visible-light images of the Helix.

alt: The Helix Nebula seen in infrared, surrounded by many background stars and galaxies.

caption: The Running Chicken Nebula, imaged by ESO's VLT Survey Telescope
story: Wispy pink plumes of gas and dust fill this vast image of the Running Chicken Nebula, known to astronomers as IC 2944. The nebula is made up of several separate clouds, and the VLT Survey Telescope, hosted at ESO's Paranal site, captured all of them.

The pink clouds glow because young, hot stars within them are lighting them up. This kind of nebula is an H II region, made of hydrogen gas that shines after being energised by the intense light of newborn stars. Gas and dust are mixed together throughout these clouds.

The image itself is enormous. It contains 1.5 billion pixels and covers an area of sky about as large as 25 full Moons. Survey telescopes like the VST are built to capture wide stretches of sky in fine detail, so a single picture can show an entire nebula along with its surroundings.

understand.summary: This visible-light image was taken with the OmegaCAM camera on ESO's VLT Survey Telescope, through u, g, r and i filters plus a hydrogen-alpha filter. The colour assigned to each filter is not published.
understand.eye: The long exposures and the hydrogen-alpha filter bring out faint glowing gas that would be very hard to see by eye.

alt: A wide field of stars with wispy pink clouds of gas and dust.

caption: LHA 120-N150 in the Tarantula Nebula, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: In this Hubble image we see LHA 120-N150, a smaller structure within the gigantic Tarantula Nebula. Among star-forming regions in the local Universe, the Tarantula is the largest known, a vast cloud where new stars are forming in large numbers.

More than 160 000 light-years from us, the nebula belongs to the Large Magellanic Cloud. That is a dwarf irregular galaxy, a small galaxy without a neat spiral or elliptical shape, and it orbits our own Milky Way as one of its neighbours.

Because the Large Magellanic Cloud is so close by astronomical standards, Hubble can study its star-forming regions in far more detail than those in more distant galaxies. Zooming in on a piece of the Tarantula like N150 lets astronomers examine one part of a huge nursery on its own, and see how its young stars sit within the surrounding gas and dust.

understand.summary: This image comes from Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3, combining visible and near-infrared filters with a hydrogen-alpha filter that traces glowing hydrogen. The colour assigned to each filter is not published.
understand.eye: Part of the light is near-infrared, invisible to the eye, and the hydrogen filter makes glowing gas stand out far more than it would to an observer.

alt: A region of gas, dust and stars within the Tarantula Nebula.

caption: The Lagoon Nebula, imaged by ESO's VLT Survey Telescope
story: This richly detailed view of the Lagoon Nebula, also known as Messier 8, comes from the VLT Survey Telescope at ESO's Paranal Observatory in Chile. The Lagoon is a giant cloud of gas and dust that is busy producing intensely bright young stars, and it is home to young clusters of stars.

Clouds like this are the birthplaces of stars. Where the gas and dust are dense enough, gravity pulls material together until new stars ignite, often in groups that form clusters. The energetic light of those young stars in turn lights up the gas around them.

This picture is only a tiny part of a much bigger project. It comes from one of eleven public surveys of the sky being carried out with ESO telescopes. Together those surveys are building up a vast store of publicly available data that astronomers anywhere in the world can use for their own research.

understand.summary: This image was taken with ESO's VLT Survey Telescope using u, g, r and i filters plus a hydrogen-alpha filter that traces glowing hydrogen. The colour assigned to each filter is not published.
understand.eye: The long exposures gather far more light than the eye, and the hydrogen-alpha filter makes the glowing gas much more prominent than it would appear by eye.

alt: The Lagoon Nebula, a large cloud of glowing gas and dust with young stars.

caption: The centre of the Lagoon Nebula, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: This Hubble close-up looks into the centre of the Lagoon Nebula, Messier 8, where delicate structures have formed in the gas. The blue-white flare at the upper left is not part of the nebula at all. It is stray light from a bright star lying just beyond the edge of the frame.

The shapes in the gas come from an encounter between young stars and the cloud of hydrogen they were born from. The newborn stars give off powerful radiation, and as it strikes the surrounding hydrogen it sculpts the gas into fine, delicate features.

Each colour is assigned to a particular kind of light. Red marks glowing hydrogen, green marks ionised nitrogen, and blue marks light through a yellow filter. Separating these gases lets astronomers see where different processes are happening in the cloud, and how the young stars are reshaping their surroundings.
explore: The picture was made with the Wide Field Channel of Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys, with exposures of 1560, 1600 and 400 seconds. It covers about 3.3 by 1.7 arcminutes of sky.

understand.summary: This image comes from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys. Glowing hydrogen (F658N) is shown in red, ionised nitrogen (F660N) in green, and light through a yellow filter (F550M) in blue.
understand.eye: The narrow filters isolate the glow of specific gases, so the colours map chemistry rather than what an eye would see.

alt: Delicate structures of glowing gas at the centre of a nebula, with a blue-white flare of light at the upper left.

caption: Part of the Omega Nebula, Messier 17, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Like a raging sea, a bubbly ocean of glowing gas fills this Hubble view of a small region inside Messier 17, also called the Omega or Swan Nebula. The nebula is a hotbed of star formation about 5500 light-years away in Sagittarius, and this patch is roughly 3 light-years across.

The wave-like shapes were sculpted and lit by a flood of ultraviolet light from young, massive stars that sit off to the upper left. Their glow reveals the three-dimensional structure of the gas. The radiation is eroding and warming the outer layers of cold hydrogen clouds, and those warmed surfaces glow orange and red.

Heat and pressure drive some material off those surfaces, forming a veil of even hotter gas, shown in green, which hides structures behind it. The pressure on the crests of the waves may be enough to trigger new stars inside them.
explore: It was released for the thirteenth anniversary of the telescope's launch.

understand.summary: This image comes from Hubble's Wide Field Planetary Camera 2. The colours represent different gases, with red for sulphur, green for hydrogen and blue for oxygen.
understand.eye: The colours are assigned to individual gases, so they map chemistry rather than the natural hues an eye would see.

alt: Wave-like clouds of glowing gas in orange, red and green, resembling a stormy sea.

caption: Herbig-Haro object HH 505 in the Orion Nebula, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Gracefully curving structures arc across the top and bottom of this colourful Hubble cloudscape. They are outflows from a young star, surrounding a Herbig-Haro object called HH 505 at the edge of the Orion Nebula, some 1000 light-years from Earth.

Herbig-Haro objects are glowing regions around newborn stars. They form when winds or jets of gas from the young star slam into nearby gas and dust at high speed, creating shockwaves. The outflows of HH 505 come from a star named IX Ori, and they are bent into winding curves as they run into the broad stream of gas and dust flowing out from the nebula's core.

The Orion Nebula is flooded with intense ultraviolet light from bright young stars. That light makes the shockwaves shine, but it also lights up slower currents of material, so astronomers studying outflows and planet-forming discs can observe the jets directly and learn about their structure.
explore: The Orion Nebula, where thousands of stars are forming, is the nearest place to Earth where massive stars are forming, so Hubble has often observed it. This view was also part of a Hubble mosaic of the nebula built from 520 images in five colours.

understand.summary: This image comes from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys, using narrow filters that isolate the glow of oxygen, hydrogen and nitrogen. The colour assigned to each filter is not published.
understand.eye: The narrow filters pick out light from specific gases, making faint outflows stand out much more than they would to an eye.

alt: Colourful clouds of gas with curving outflow structures at the top and bottom of the image.

caption: The Cat's Paw and Lobster Nebulae, imaged by ESO's VLT Survey Telescope
story: The Cat's Paw Nebula, NGC 6334, at upper right, and the Lobster Nebula, NGC 6357, at lower left, share this giant image from the VLT Survey Telescope. Their gas glows red, and dark clouds of dust weave through the very rich star field around them.

Both are regions of active star formation. Hot young stars inside them are pouring out energetic light that makes the surrounding hydrogen gas shine red, the characteristic glow of hydrogen that has been energised in this way.

The picture is huge, with around two billion pixels, making it one of the largest images ESO has released. That scale lets viewers zoom from the full sweep of both nebulae right down to small details within them. The circular features around bright stars are not real, though. They are reflections inside the optics of the telescope and camera.

understand.summary: This image was made with the OmegaCAM camera on ESO's VLT Survey Telescope, using g and r filters and a narrow-band filter. The colour assigned to each filter is not published.
understand.eye: The long exposures gather far more light than the eye, so the red glow and dark dust clouds appear much more vivid than they would to an observer.

alt: Two nebulae glowing red, one at upper right and one at lower left, among many stars and dark dust clouds.

caption: The Skull and Crossbones Nebula, NGC 2467, imaged by ESO's Very Large Telescope
story: Dust, gas and bright young stars seem to form a grinning skull in this picture of NGC 2467, a nebula nicknamed the Skull and Crossbones. It is an active star-forming region, and the image was captured with the FORS instrument on ESO's Very Large Telescope.

In a star-forming region, clouds of gas and dust collapse under gravity to make new stars. Once those stars switch on, their intense light energises the surrounding gas and makes it glow. In NGC 2467 they happen to be arranged so that the whole thing suggests a face.

ESO's telescopes are normally busy collecting data for scientific research. Their immense resolving power, though, also makes them well suited to capturing images like this one, which are valued simply for their own beauty.

understand.summary: This visible-light image comes from the FORS2 instrument on ESO's Very Large Telescope, using b, v and R filters plus a hydrogen-alpha filter. The colour assigned to each filter is not published.
understand.eye: The long exposure and hydrogen-alpha filter bring out faint glowing gas much more clearly than an eye could see it.

alt: A nebula of gas, dust and bright young stars arranged in a shape resembling a grinning skull.

caption: Supernova remnant E0102 in the Small Magellanic Cloud, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
captureDate: Hubble ACS data 2003; WFPC2 oxygen images 1995
story: A greenish-blue shell of debris sits just below the centre of this Hubble image, much like fireworks. It is E0102, formally 1E0102.2-7219, what remains after a massive star exploded as a supernova in the Small Magellanic Cloud, a nearby dwarf galaxy. In the upper right glows the star-forming region N 76, a delicate structure in lavender and peach hues.
The two look different because of what they are made of. N 76 shines mainly with glowing hydrogen. E0102 is an oxygen-rich remnant, with a great deal of oxygen and very little hydrogen or helium.

One explanation is that the star that exploded had already blown most of its hydrogen away in a stellar wind. It may have been a Wolf-Rayet star, a type that can be upward of 20 times the Sun's mass and famous for strong winds, which strip away outer shells and leave oxygen behind.
explore: E0102 is only about 2000 years old, young enough that astronomers can study material from a massive star's core directly. It lies almost 50 light-years from the edge of N 76.
The Small Magellanic Cloud is visible from the Southern Hemisphere towards Tucana and lies roughly 210,000 light-years away.

understand.summary: This image combines 2003 data from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys, through blue, visible, infrared and hydrogen filters, with oxygen images from the Wide Field Planetary Camera 2. The colour assigned to each filter is not published.
understand.eye: Narrow filters isolate the glow of specific gases like oxygen and hydrogen, so the colours map chemistry more than what an eye would see.

alt: A greenish-blue shell of debris below centre, with a glowing lavender and peach cloud in the upper right.

caption: Star-forming region Lupus 3, imaged by ESO's VLT Survey Telescope and the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope
story: Snaking across this wide view is a dark cloud of dust, lit by the brilliant light of newly formed stars. This dense cloud is Lupus 3, a star-forming region where very hot stars are being born from collapsing masses of gas and dust.

Stars begin life inside clouds like this one. Where the gas and dust are packed densely enough, gravity pulls material inward until it becomes hot and dense enough for a new star to ignite. The cloud looks dark because its dust blocks the light of the stars behind it, while the young stars nearby shine brightly beside it.

The picture was assembled from images taken with two ESO telescopes, the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope and the VLT Survey Telescope. According to ESO, the result is the most detailed image yet made of this region, giving astronomers a sharp look at a place where stars are forming.

understand.summary: This visible-light image was assembled from data taken with ESO's VLT Survey Telescope and the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope. The filter list also includes blue and red Digitized Sky Survey 2 data. The colour assigned to each filter is not published.
understand.eye: The long exposures gather far more light than the eye, revealing the texture of the dark cloud and faint light around the young stars.

alt: A dark, winding cloud of dust across a field of stars, with bright young stars lighting it.

caption: Reflection nebula around the star HD 87643, imaged by the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope
story: An extended nebula of gas and dust surrounds the star HD 87643 at the centre of this image, reflecting the star's light back towards us. Bright, ragged tendrils of gas and dust stretch through it.
HD 87643 is a B[e] star, an unusual type of hot star surrounded by gas and dust. The wind flowing from the central star appears to have shaped the nebula, sweeping it into tattered tendrils.

Looking closely at those features has given astronomers a clue to the star's behaviour. A careful study of them seems to show that the star throws off matter at regular intervals, every 15 to 50 years. Those repeated episodes are written into the structure of the nebula around it. ESO's MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope at La Silla captured the image with its Wide Field Imager, combining data taken through three filters, B, V and R.

understand.summary: This visible-light image was made with the Wide Field Imager on the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope through B, V and R filters. The colour assigned to each filter is not published.
understand.eye: The long exposures gather far more light than the eye, bringing out the faint reflected glow of the nebula.

alt: A bright star at the centre of a nebula of gas and dust with ragged, bright tendrils.

caption: The Omega Nebula, Messier 17, imaged by ESO's Very Large Telescope
story: Vast clouds of gas and dust, lit by the intense radiation of young stars, give this view of Messier 17 the look of a painting. The nebula, also called the Omega or Swan Nebula, lies in Sagittarius, the Archer, about 6000 light-years from Earth. The central region pictured is about 15 light-years across, while the whole nebula spans about 40 light-years.

At the centre is a cluster of massive young stars whose radiation makes the surrounding hydrogen glow. To its lower right lies a huge cloud of molecular gas. In visible light its dust blocks the view, but in infrared the hydrogen glow behind it shines faintly through.

Hidden in that dark reddish region, astronomers found the silhouette of an opaque disc of gas and dust. It looks small but is about 20 000 AU across, dwarfing our Solar System. The disc is thought to be rotating and feeding material onto a protostar, a star in the making.
explore: One AU equals the average Earth-Sun distance. Messier 17 is also a popular target for amateur astronomers, who can capture good images of it with small telescopes.

understand.summary: This near-infrared image was made with the ISAAC instrument on ESO's Very Large Telescope. The J filter (1.25 microns) is shown in blue, H (1.6 microns) in green and K (2.2 microns) in red.
understand.eye: All three bands are infrared, invisible to the eye, and infrared light passes through dust that blocks visible light, revealing glowing gas hidden from ordinary view.

alt: Clouds of gas and dust around a central cluster of bright young stars, with a dark reddish cloud to the lower right.

caption: Part of the Vela supernova remnant, imaged by ESO's VLT Survey Telescope
story: Pink and orange filaments swirl across this picture, suggesting the ghostly shape of a giant bird, with orange wings spread wide, a long pink body and one bright pinkish star for an eye. Countless stars are sprinkled all around. What we are seeing is one small patch of the Vela supernova remnant, the tangled debris of a massive star that exploded 11 000 years ago.

When massive stars reach the end of their lives, they explode as supernovae and hurl their outer layers into space. The blast drives shock waves through the surrounding gas, squeezing and reshaping it. That is what created this web of filaments, which still shine because of the energy the explosion released.

The constellation of Vela is visible without a telescope from the southern sky, but details like these are far beyond what the eye can pick out. This view is part of a huge, detailed mosaic made with the VLT Survey Telescope at ESO's Paranal Observatory in the Chilean desert.

understand.summary: This visible-light image was taken with the OmegaCAM camera on ESO's VLT Survey Telescope, through u, g, r and i filters plus a hydrogen-alpha filter. The colour assigned to each filter is not published.
understand.eye: The caption notes that Vela's stars are visible to the naked eye, but these faint filaments only emerge in long telescope exposures.

alt: Pink and orange filaments of gas shaped like a bird with spread wings, among many stars.

caption: Supernova 1987A, imaged by ALMA, the Hubble Space Telescope and the Chandra X-ray Observatory
story: This composite image shows the remains of SN 1987A, a supernova in the Large Magellanic Cloud, a satellite galaxy of the Milky Way. It combines observations from ALMA, the NASA/ESA Hubble Space Telescope and NASA's Chandra X-ray Observatory.

The explosion was discovered on 23 February 1987. It was one of the brightest supernovae seen in more than 400 years, blazing for several months with the power of 100 million suns. As the nearest supernova observed in centuries, it quickly became the most thoroughly studied of all time. Decades of follow-up from space and the ground have let astronomers trace a massive star's death step by step, from star to supernova to remnant.

For several years now, ALMA has been studying the glowing debris in high resolution at millimetre and submillimetre wavelengths. It shows the remnant forming vast amounts of dust from new elements made in the original star.
explore: Some of this dust will drift into interstellar space and may one day become material for planets around other stars. The findings hint that similar explosions produced the dust of the early Universe.

understand.summary: This composite combines millimetre-wave data from ALMA, visible light from Hubble and X-rays from Chandra. The colour assigned to each dataset is not published.
understand.eye: X-rays and millimetre waves are completely invisible to the eye, so much of what appears here could never be seen directly.

alt: A composite image of the supernova remnant SN 1987A.

caption: The Serpens Nebula, imaged by the HAWK-I instrument on ESO's Very Large Telescope
story: The Serpens Nebula was imaged by HAWK-I, an instrument installed on ESO's Very Large Telescope, operated by the European Southern Observatory. The nebula lies about 1300 light-years away.

The Serpens Nebula is a reflection nebula. Unlike nebulae that shine with their own glowing gas, a reflection nebula is a cloud of dust that scatters the light of nearby stars back towards us, a little like fog lit up by car headlights.

The filters HAWK-I used to make this picture cover wavelengths similar to those of filters used by the Hubble Space Telescope. That similarity is useful. When two telescopes observe the same object in comparable light, astronomers can set their images side by side and compare what each one reveals about the region.

understand.summary: This image comes from the HAWK-I instrument on ESO's Very Large Telescope, using filters similar in wavelength to Hubble's. The specific filters and colour mapping are not published.
understand.eye: A long telescope exposure gathers far more light than the eye, so faint reflected light in the nebula becomes visible.

alt: The Serpens Nebula as seen by the HAWK-I instrument.

caption: Emission nebula NGC 6188, imaged by the ESO 3.6-metre telescope
story: This image shows the emission nebula NGC 6188, photographed long ago with ESO's 3.6-metre telescope at the La Silla observatory in Chile. The nebula lies about 4,000 light-years away in the southern constellation of Ara.

An emission nebula is a cloud of gas that gives off its own light rather than simply reflecting the light of nearby stars. In NGC 6188, the light comes from within. Stars embedded in the nebula emit radiation that heats the gases around them, and the energised gas glows in response. Without those stars, the cloud would stay dark.
Because the picture is an old one, it is also a piece of ESO's own history, taken with one of the telescopes at La Silla long before many of the images in this collection.

understand.summary: This image was taken with the ESO 3.6-metre telescope at La Silla. The filters and colour mapping are not published.
understand.eye: A long telescope exposure gathers far more light than the eye, so the nebula's faint glow appears far brighter than it would to an observer.

alt: The glowing emission nebula NGC 6188.

caption: The Southern Ring Nebula, NGC 3132, imaged by ESO
story: This picture shows NGC 3132, a planetary nebula also known as the Eight-Burst or the Southern Ring Nebula. It shines about 2,000 light-years away in the constellation of Vela, which makes it one of the nearest objects of its kind.

A planetary nebula forms near the end of a star's life, when the star sheds its outer layers of gas into space. The core left behind gives off radiation that makes the expelled shell of gas glow, producing a round, bubble-like cloud.

Despite the name, these objects have nothing to do with planets. The term comes from their appearance through small telescopes, where their round shapes made them look a little like the planets of our Solar System. The name stuck even after astronomers understood that they are really the glowing outer layers of dying stars, spreading slowly outward from what remains of the star at the centre.

understand.summary: This image was released by ESO. The telescope, filters and colour mapping are not published.
understand.eye: A long telescope exposure gathers far more light than the eye, so the glowing shell appears brighter and more detailed than it would through a small telescope.

alt: The planetary nebula NGC 3132, a glowing shell of gas.

caption: Part of the Cygnus Loop supernova remnant, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: This Hubble image shows a small portion of the Cygnus Loop, the remains of a colossal stellar explosion. It was taken with Hubble's Wide Field and Planetary Camera.

The Cygnus Loop traces the rim of a bubble-shaped blast wave that is still expanding outward from a star that exploded about 15,000 years ago. A supernova hurls the outer layers of a star into space, and as that material and the shock wave in front of it plough into surrounding gas, they heat it and make it glow.

Seeing only a small section of the remnant is useful. Zooming in on the edge of the blast wave lets astronomers look closely at the boundary where the explosion meets the gas between the stars, and study how the shock is moving through it. This stretch of the blast wave is still expanding, so the scene is slowly changing.

understand.summary: This image was taken with Hubble's Wide Field and Planetary Camera. The filters and colour mapping are not published.
understand.eye: A long telescope exposure gathers far more light than the eye, revealing faint structure along the blast wave.

alt: A small section of the glowing edge of the Cygnus Loop supernova remnant.

caption: The heart of the Trifid Nebula, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: This Hubble image looks into the heart of the Trifid Nebula, catalogued by astronomers as Messier 20 or NGC 6514. It is a well-known region of star formation inside our own Milky Way, lying in the direction of the constellation of Sagittarius.

The nebula owes its name to its appearance in small telescopes. Three bands of dark interstellar dust lie across it, dividing it into three parts. That dust blocks the light of the glowing gas behind it, producing the dark lanes.

In a star-forming region like this, clouds of gas and dust collapse to form new stars, and the energetic light of those young stars in turn makes the surrounding gas glow. Hubble's camera recorded this glow through separate filters for oxygen, hydrogen and sulphur, each isolating light from a single gas. Separating them this way helps astronomers map the conditions across the nebula and see how young stars are shaping it.

understand.summary: This image comes from Hubble's Wide Field Planetary Camera 2, using narrow filters for oxygen, hydrogen-alpha and sulphur. The colour assigned to each filter is not published.
understand.eye: The narrow filters isolate light from individual gases, so the colours map chemistry rather than what an eye would see.

scaleExtra: The Trifid Nebula lies about 9,000 light-years from Earth, according to ESA/Hubble.
alt: The central region of the Trifid Nebula.

caption: The 30 Doradus star-forming region, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope and the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope
story: This panoramic view shows 30 Doradus, also known as the Tarantula Nebula, the brightest star-forming region in our galactic neighbourhood. It is home to the most massive stars ever seen, and it sits in the Large Magellanic Cloud, a small galaxy orbiting the Milky Way, 170 000 light-years from us.

No star-forming region we know of inside our own galaxy is as large or as productive as 30 Doradus. That makes it a natural laboratory for studying how big, heavy stars are born and how they shape the gas clouds around them.

The picture is one of the largest mosaics ever put together from Hubble photos. It stitches together observations from two Hubble cameras, the Advanced Camera for Surveys and Wide Field Camera 3, and adds data from the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope of the European Southern Observatory, which traces where hydrogen and oxygen gas are glowing across the region.
explore: The image was released to celebrate Hubble's 22nd anniversary.

understand.summary: This mosaic combines Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 and Advanced Camera for Surveys with the Wide Field Imager on the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope, whose narrow filters trace glowing hydrogen and oxygen. The colour assigned to each filter is not published.
understand.eye: Narrow filters isolate the glow of particular gases and the long exposures gather far more light than the eye, so the nebula appears far richer than it would to an observer.

alt: A wide panorama of the 30 Doradus star-forming region.

caption: Star-forming region NGC 3603 and its central cluster, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: This Hubble view shows NGC 3603, a rich region of star formation, together with the massive, compact cluster of stars at its centre. The picture was taken with Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys. A box on the image marks the area that astronomers studied in detail.

That boxed region was used to detect how the stars inside the cluster are moving. Measuring such motion takes precise observations, because stars in a cluster shift their positions only very slightly from one image to the next.

A star cluster is a group of stars born together from the same cloud of gas and dust. In a massive, compact cluster like this one, the stars are packed tightly into a small space. Tracking their movements helps astronomers understand how the cluster holds together under its own gravity, and what may happen to it as it ages, whether it stays bound or its stars gradually drift apart into the wider galaxy.

understand.summary: This image was taken with Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys through blue, visible and near-infrared filters. The colour assigned to each filter is not published.
understand.eye: Part of the light is near-infrared, invisible to the eye, and Hubble's sharp view helps separate stars in the crowded cluster.

alt: A star-forming region with a compact central cluster of stars, with a box drawn around the studied area.

caption: The core of globular cluster 47 Tucanae, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: This Hubble image shows the crowded core of 47 Tucanae, a globular cluster, a dense ball of stars. Repeated photographs of this region let astronomers follow the 'beehive swarm' motion of its stars, and they measured precise speeds for nearly 15,000 of them.

The work was part of a seven-year study using Hubble. It gave astronomers their strongest observational evidence so far that globular clusters sort their stars by mass. The sorting works like a game of gravitational billiards. As stars pass near one another, heavier stars lose speed and sink towards the core, while lighter stars gain speed and move out towards the edges.

This process is known as mass segregation. Astronomers had long suspected that it happens in globular clusters, but it had never before been directly observed in action. Tracking thousands of individual stars over years finally made that possible.

understand.summary: This image was taken with Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys through blue, visible and near-infrared filters. The colour assigned to each filter is not published.
understand.eye: Part of the light is near-infrared, invisible to the eye, and repeated sharp Hubble images let astronomers track individual stars in the crowded core.

alt: The densely packed core of a globular cluster filled with stars.

caption: Globular cluster NGC 6397, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Hundreds of thousands of stars glitter in this Hubble portrait of NGC 6397, an ancient globular cluster. Blue stars are scattered among them, a reddish glow comes from other stars, and a myriad of small white points fill the rest of the frame.

The colours reflect the stars' life stages. The blue stars are nearing the end of their lives. They have used up the hydrogen fuel that made them shine and now convert helium to energy in their cores, which burns hotter and makes them appear blue. The reddish glow comes from red giants, stars that have also run through their hydrogen and swelled in size. Many of the small white objects are stars like our Sun.

Astronomers used Hubble to measure the cluster's distance at 7800 light-years, making it one of the nearest globular clusters to Earth. The distance measurement was made with Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3.
explore: The image itself was built from a series of observations taken between July 2004 and June 2005 with Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys.

understand.summary: This image was taken with Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys through blue and red filters. The colour assigned to each filter is not published.
understand.eye: Hubble's sharp view picks out myriad individual stars, and the exposures gather far more light than an eye could.

alt: A dense cluster of stars with scattered blue stars, reddish stars and many small white points.

caption: The core of globular cluster M13, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Many hundreds of thousands of stars crowd this Hubble view of the globular cluster M13, caught in a single instant as they move about. Among the globular clusters of the northern sky, M13 is one of the brightest and most familiar, and it is easy to find in the constellation of Hercules.

A globular cluster is a dense, ball-shaped swarm of old stars held together by gravity. Near the centre the stars are packed especially closely, and Hubble's sharp vision can separate many of them into individual points of light.

This picture was not made from one observation. It is a composite of archival Hubble data from four separate science proposals, gathered with two Hubble cameras, WFPC2 and the Advanced Camera for Surveys. Broadband filters isolated light from the blue, visible and infrared parts of the spectrum.
explore: ESA/Hubble describes this glittering metropolis of stars as easy to spot in the winter sky.

understand.summary: This composite combines archival data from Hubble's Wide Field Planetary Camera 2 and Advanced Camera for Surveys, through blue, visible and near-infrared filters. The colour assigned to each filter is not published.
understand.eye: Part of the light is near-infrared, invisible to the eye, and Hubble's sharp view picks out individual stars in the crowded centre.

alt: The dense centre of a globular cluster packed with hundreds of thousands of stars.

caption: The shell around the cool red star U Antliae, imaged by ALMA
story: This ALMA image shows a delicate shell of material around the cool red star U Antliae, in finer detail than has ever been possible before.

The shell records a brief, violent episode in the star's life. Some 2700 years ago, the star briefly lost mass very rapidly. In a period lasting only a few hundred years, it threw off, at high speed, the material that now makes up the shell.

Looking at the shell more closely reveals some evidence of thin, wispy clouds within it, known as filamentary substructures. Studying fine features like these helps astronomers understand how stars like U Antliae shed their material into space. ALMA can do this because it observes at millimetre wavelengths, which pick up cool gas that does not glow in visible light.

understand.summary: This image was made with the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) in its Band 6, at a wavelength of about 1.3 millimetres. The colour mapping is not published.
understand.eye: Millimetre-wave light is invisible to the eye, so this view of the shell cannot be seen directly.

alt: A thin, delicate shell of material surrounding a star.

caption: Globular cluster Terzan 5, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: This Hubble image shows the ancient globular cluster Terzan 5, deep within the Milky Way, in fine detail. What makes it especially interesting to astronomers, though, is not how it looks but the chaotic way its stars are moving.

Terzan 5 has an exceptionally dense core, so stars there are thought to collide more often than in almost any other globular cluster. With stars crammed together so tightly, many are pushed close enough to form tight pairs called binary systems.

Studies of individual stars have turned up a surprise. They fall into two separate age groups, one about 6 billion years old and the other about 12 billion. Some astronomers have suggested the younger group could have been pulled from a dwarf galaxy, though this remains a hypothesis.
explore: The picture was made with the Wide Field Channel of Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys, with total exposures of 340 and 360 seconds per filter. It covers 3.1 by 1.4 arcminutes of sky.

understand.summary: This image comes from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys. Light through a yellow-red filter (F606W) is coloured blue and near-infrared light (F814W) is coloured red.
understand.eye: The red channel records near-infrared light, invisible to the eye, and the colours are assigned rather than natural.

alt: A dense cluster of many stars packed closely together.

caption: Hot blue stars at the core of globular cluster M15, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: This Hubble image looks into the centre of the globular cluster M15. In it, astronomers found about 15 very hot stars not seen before, sitting isolated at the cluster's core.

A globular cluster is a dense ball of stars held together by gravity, and its core is the most crowded part of all. That crowding may account for these unusual stars. The most likely explanation is that they are 'naked cores', stars that have been stripped of their outer envelopes of gas, exposing the hot interiors underneath.

For that to happen, the stars in the cluster's core must be so tightly packed that they can pull material off one another through gravity. Finding these stars therefore says something about conditions at the heart of M15, where stars crowd together closely enough to interfere with one another directly. That is very different from the Sun's surroundings, where neighbouring stars are far apart.

understand.summary: This image was taken with the Hubble Space Telescope. The instrument, filters and colour mapping are not published.
understand.eye: Hubble's sharp view helps separate individual stars in the crowded core.

alt: The crowded centre of a globular cluster.

caption: The Milky Way and Nova Centauri 2013, La Silla Observatory, Chile
story: The southern Milky Way crosses this view of the night sky above ESO's La Silla Observatory, a sea of stars from edge to edge. On the left stands the Swedish-ESO Submillimetre Telescope, known as SEST.

Among all those stars, one is special and shining brightly. It is Nova Centauri 2013, also known as V1369 Centauri. A nova is a star system that suddenly flares up far brighter than normal, then gradually fades back over time. When that happens, a star that was once hard to see can briefly stand out in the sky.
The telescopes at La Silla are built to watch the heavens, and on this night the camera caught the southern Milky Way with a newly brightened star among its crowd.

understand.summary: This is a landscape photograph at ESO's La Silla Observatory, in visible light. The camera settings and colour processing are not published.
understand.eye: A camera exposure can gather far more light than the eye, so the Milky Way may look richer and brighter than it would to someone standing there.

alt: The Milky Way stretching across a starry sky above La Silla Observatory, with the Swedish-ESO Submillimetre Telescope on the left.

caption: Star trails over the ESO 3.6-metre telescope, La Silla Observatory, Chile
story: Stars trace long arcs across the sky above the ESO 3.6-metre telescope in this photograph. The trails form because the camera's shutter stays open while the Earth turns, so each star draws a curved line rather than appearing as a point.

Beneath them, the telescope is home to HARPS (the High Accuracy Radial velocity Planet Searcher), which ESO describes as the world's foremost exoplanet hunter. Instead of taking pictures of planets, instruments like HARPS look for the tiny back-and-forth wobble a planet causes in its star as the two orbit each other.

This image was shared through the Your ESO Pictures Flickr Group, a place where anyone can submit photos connected with ESO. That openness lets many different photographers share their own views of ESO's telescopes under the night sky.

understand.summary: This is a landscape photograph taken at ESO's La Silla Observatory, in visible light. The camera settings and colour processing are not published.
understand.eye: The eye sees stars as fixed points. Only a long exposure turns the Earth's rotation into visible trails.

alt: Curved star trails arcing across the night sky above the ESO 3.6-metre telescope.

caption: Swirling star trails above the Very Large Telescope, Paranal Observatory, Chile
story: Stars appear to swirl in circles above the enclosures of ESO's Very Large Telescope at Paranal in this photograph of the rotating night sky.

The stars are not really moving in loops. The effect comes from a very long exposure, with the photographer keeping the camera's shutter open while the Earth turned beneath the sky. As our planet rotates, the stars seem to glide slowly across the heavens, and over a long exposure each one leaves a curved streak of light in the image.

The result turns a still scene into a record of time passing. The telescope enclosures stay fixed and sharp in the foreground, because they turn along with the Earth, while the sky behind them wheels around. Every observation made from the ground is taken from a spinning platform, and telescopes must steadily track the stars to keep them in view.

caption: The Milky Way arching over the Paranal Residencia, Paranal Observatory, Chile
story: The Milky Way arches across the sky above ESO's Paranal Observatory in this panorama. Up from the desert in the foreground rises the familiar glass dome of the Paranal Residencia.

Towards the horizon, the sky is tinged with a mixture of soft red and green hues. This glow is called airglow, a faint light given off by the Earth's upper atmosphere itself. It fills the lower sky near the horizon, over the open desert landscape.

Set within those glows are the Large and Small Magellanic Clouds, two small galaxies that are neighbours of the Milky Way. Below them, under the arch of our own galaxy, sits the Residencia's rounded glass dome, with the observatory's telescopes nearby to study that same sky.

caption: Cerro Armazones at night, Chile
story: This night-time image was taken at ESO's Astronomical Site Monitor on Cerro Armazones, a mountain in the Chilean desert close to Paranal Observatory, home of the Very Large Telescope.

When this picture was released, Cerro Armazones was one of about half a dozen candidate sites for the Extremely Large Telescope, or ELT. With a mirror in the 40-metre class, the ELT was described as set to become the world's biggest eye on the sky.

Choosing a site for a telescope like that is a careful process. An ELT Site Selection Advisory Committee reviewed the options, and Cerro Armazones came out as its recommended site on the final shortlist. The committee chose it for two reasons, the mountain's excellent sky quality and the fact that its operation could be integrated with the existing observatory at nearby Paranal. Being close to an established site means the two can share operations rather than starting from scratch.

caption: The Milky Way beside an Auxiliary Telescope, Paranal Observatory, Chile
story: The Milky Way stretches across the sky next to one of the four 1.8-metre Auxiliary Telescopes at ESO's Paranal Observatory, in a photograph taken during the ESO Ultra HD Expedition.

These smaller telescopes do not work only on their own. Together with the four Unit Telescopes, whose main mirrors are 8.2 m across, they can be linked to form a giant 'interferometer' called the ESO Very Large Telescope Interferometer. By combining the light collected by several telescopes spread out on the mountain, an interferometer can see far finer detail than any one of them could manage alone.

ESO describes the combination as the world's most advanced optical instrument for exploring the depths of the Universe. On this night the Auxiliary Telescope stands beneath the band of the Milky Way, part of the galaxy it helps astronomers to study.

caption: Star trails over the Swedish-ESO Submillimetre Telescope, La Silla Observatory, Chile
story: This night shot at ESO's La Silla Observatory shows the Swedish-ESO Submillimetre Telescope, known as SEST, with the ESO 3.6-metre telescope in the background. ESO titled the picture 'Star trails at La Silla', and the trails of stars sweep across the sky above the two instruments.
Star trails appear when a camera gathers light over a long period while the Earth turns. The stars seem to wheel across the sky, and the camera records that motion as streaks instead of points.

The two telescopes are very different. SEST, as its name says, was built to observe submillimetre light, a kind of radiation well beyond what our eyes can detect. ESO Photo Ambassador Yuri Beletsky took the photograph as part of the ESO Ultra High Definition Expedition.

caption: Star trails over the desert near Paranal Observatory, Chile
story: Stars leave long, curving paths across the sky in this view from the desert around ESO's Paranal Observatory in Chile. These star trails all seem to circle around a single fixed point, the Earth's Celestial South Pole, seen just above a rust-tinted horizon.

The stars are not really travelling around that point. The effect is caused by the Earth's rotation. As our planet spins, the sky appears to turn around us, and a camera gathering light over a long time records each star as a curved streak rather than a dot.

The point at the centre of the circles is where the Earth's axis points into the southern sky. Stars close to it trace small circles, while those farther away sweep out wider arcs. A long exposure turns that everyday motion, too slow to notice by eye, into a visible pattern.

caption: Stars distorted by hot air above Paranal Observatory, Chile
story: The night sky in this photograph looks strangely warped and smeared. The cause is hot air rising from a chimney, which blurs and distorts the stars behind it.

The chimney belongs to the generator that keeps ESO's Paranal Observatory running. Because Paranal is too remote for Chile's power grid to reach, the observatory depends entirely on its own power station.

The distortion is a vivid, close-up version of a problem astronomers face all the time. Warm and cool pockets of air bend light slightly differently, so starlight passing through moving air gets jostled on its way to the ground. In this case the effect is exaggerated by the hot exhaust right in front of the camera, but a gentler version of the same thing makes stars twinkle and limits how sharp telescopes on the ground can be. That is one reason observatories are built at high, dry sites where the air above is as calm as possible.

understand.eye: Someone standing there might see stars shimmer through the hot air, but a camera exposure records that distortion as a frozen smear.

caption: Yepun's laser and the Magellanic Clouds, Paranal Observatory, Chile
story: A powerful yellow laser beam shoots into the sky from Yepun, the fourth 8.2-metre Unit Telescope of ESO's Very Large Telescope. To the left of the beam is the Large Magellanic Cloud and to the right the Small Magellanic Cloud, nearby dwarf galaxies easily seen with the unaided eye from the southern hemisphere.

The laser is there for a reason. Earth's atmosphere blurs everything ground-based telescopes observe, so astronomers use adaptive optics, in which computer-controlled mirrors change shape hundreds of times per second to cancel out the distortion.

The beam excites a layer of sodium atoms 90 km up, creating a glowing spot, an artificial star. Light returning from this Laser Guide Star is used as a reference to steer the deformable mirrors, giving images nearly as crisp as those a telescope in space would take.
explore: Left of the Large Magellanic Cloud shines Canopus, the brightest star in Carina, and the one towards the upper right is Achernar, the brightest in Eridanus. Babak Tafreshi, an ESO Photo Ambassador, took the picture.
The VLT's Unit Telescopes carry names in Mapudungun, the Mapuche language. They are Antu (the Sun), Kueyen (the Moon), Melipal (the Southern Cross) and Yepun (Venus).

caption: ALMA antennas and the centre of the Milky Way, Chajnantor plateau, Chile
story: Several of the antennas of the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array, ALMA, stand beneath the central regions of the Milky Way in this wide-field view. At the upper right glows the zodiacal light, at the lower left shines the planet Mars, and Saturn sits a little higher, towards the middle.
The zodiacal light is a faint glow caused by sunlight scattering off dust in the Solar System. It shows up best from very dark places.

The antennas themselves are built to observe the sky at millimetre and submillimetre wavelengths, light far beyond what our eyes can detect. That makes for an interesting contrast, since the camera records the visible sky while the dishes below are tuned to a completely different view of it. The picture was taken during the ESO Ultra HD Expedition.

caption: Telescopes along the road at La Silla Observatory, Chile
story: A dense scattering of stars fills the sky above the road to ESO's La Silla Observatory in Chile's Atacama Desert, lined with a variety of telescopes. The Danish 1.54-metre telescope stands in the foreground, the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope beyond it, and, furthest back, ESO's New Technology Telescope (NTT).

The Danish telescope is at work, and it has made many discoveries, including the afterglows of short gamma-ray bursts, which are probably the result of two neutron stars colliding. The 2.2-metre telescope also hunts these afterglows with its GROND instrument, flagging them for larger telescopes to follow up.

The NTT may look like a speck, but it made key advances. Big mirrors sag under their own weight and need constant adjustment to stay sharp. The NTT was the first telescope to make these corrections on the fly, keeping watch on a reference star. Called active optics, the method is now widely used in large professional telescopes.
explore: Besides GROND, the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope also carries a spectrograph, plus a wide-field camera that has produced many fine pictures of the sky.
