caption: The Pleiades and Orion over ALMA, Chajnantor plateau, Chile
story: ALMA's antennas, part of the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array, stand under a sky crowded with stars in this photograph by ESO Photo Ambassador Babak Tafreshi. In the upper left corner glows a tight bunch of young stars, the Pleiades cluster, surprisingly bright. The constellation of Orion, the Hunter, hangs over the nearest antenna, and the three blue stars just left of the red light form his belt.
The clear skies over the Chajnantor Plateau show thousands of stars to the naked eye. That dry, transparent air is one of the reasons ALMA was built here.

The scene also carries an old story. The Pleiades were known to most ancient civilisations, and in classical mythology Orion was a hunter who pursued the Pleiades, the daughters of Atlas. Through the thin air over the Atacama, it almost looks as if the chase is really taking place.
explore: ESO calls ALMA the biggest astronomical project in the world. Europe, North America and East Asia run it jointly, in cooperation with the Republic of Chile, with each region's share led by ESO, the National Radio Astronomy Observatory and the National Astronomical Observatory of Japan.

caption: Total lunar eclipse above the Very Large Telescope, Paranal Observatory, Chile
story: The eclipsed Moon hangs just above the domes of ESO's Very Large Telescope, as if the telescope were holding it up, like Atlas supporting the sky in Greek myth. The Moon glows faintly in the early morning twilight during a total lunar eclipse over Paranal Observatory in Chile's Atacama Desert.

The shot took careful planning. Astrophotographer Yuri Beletsky used precise calculations to find a spot nine kilometres east of Paranal, where the setting, eclipsed Moon would briefly line up just over the telescope domes.

A total lunar eclipse happens when the Earth passes directly between the Sun and the Moon. The Earth's shadow blocks direct sunlight, so the only light reaching the Moon has been bent through Earth's atmosphere, which gives it a reddish colour. Because that light has been filtered by our atmosphere, astronomers use eclipses to study the signatures life leaves in an atmosphere, useful in the search for life on other planets.
explore: ESO picked the photograph to illustrate April in one of its annual calendars.

caption: The Milky Way over ALMA antennas, Chajnantor plateau, Chile
story: The vast, bright ripple of the Milky Way slices the sky in two above Chile's Chajnantor plateau. Beneath its glow, a cluster of white antennas points upward, lit by a bright yellow light that tells technicians whether it is safe to approach. From the southern hemisphere, the rich centre of our galaxy is often right overhead, stretching from horizon to horizon.

The antennas belong to ALMA, the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array, a giant interferometer of 66 antennas that work together across distances of up to 16 kilometres. ALMA observes light the eye cannot see, at wavelengths of around a millimetre, between infrared and radio. This light is given off by the coldest, most remote parts of the cosmos, such as clouds of gas and dust between the stars and the most ancient galaxies.
This light is heavily absorbed by water vapour, so telescopes must sit on very high, dry sites. At over 5000 metres, the plateau is ideal.
explore: Studying this cold, faint light lets ALMA explore how stars and planets form and change over time, revealing objects and processes that had never been seen before.

caption: Laser beams from Unit Telescope 4, Paranal Observatory, Chile
story: Framed against the star-filled sky of Paranal, UT4, one of the four 8-m telescopes of ESO's Very Large Telescope, pierces the night with four laser beams from inside its dome.

The lasers come from the 4 Laser Guide Star Facility, which UT4 uses to make its own artificial stars. The beams excite sodium atoms about 90 km above the ground, making them glow. The telescope studies how these guide stars are smeared by the atmosphere, the same turbulence that makes stars twinkle, and works out how to compensate.

The corrections are carried out by UT4's adaptive optics system, which precisely reshapes the telescope's secondary mirror to cancel the atmospheric disturbances it measures. With adaptive optics, a telescope on the ground can take far sharper images than the air would normally allow, nearly as good as sending the VLT into space.
explore: The other three 8-m telescopes are due to get one laser each, as part of upgrades to the VLT Interferometer and its GRAVITY+ instrument, which combines light from several telescopes into a huge 'virtual' telescope.
ESO's Extremely Large Telescope, being built not far from Paranal, will have at least 6 lasers.

caption: Star trails over La Silla Observatory, Chile
story: Circles of starlight wheel around the south celestial pole, seen directly overhead at ESO's La Silla Observatory in this dizzying photograph by ESO Photo Ambassador Alexandre Santerne. At first glance it could pass for an optical illusion or an abstract painting.

Each circular streak is one star, recorded over a long period so that its apparent motion across the sky, caused by the Earth's rotation, becomes visible. La Silla sits on the outskirts of Chile's Atacama Desert some 2400 metres up, and enjoys over 300 clear nights a year, ideal for long exposures like this.

Several telescopes appear near the bottom. The ESO 3.6-metre telescope stands on the left peak and hosts HARPS, the High Accuracy Radial velocity Planet Searcher, which ESO calls the world's foremost extrasolar planet hunter. The New Technology Telescope partly hides it, and the silver-domed MPG/ESO 2.2-metre is visible too.
explore: Other telescopes in view include the Swiss 1.2-metre Leonhard Euler Telescope, the ESO 1-metre Schmidt, the Danish 1.54-metre and the ESO 1.52-metre.
ESO ranks La Silla just behind the VLT among the world's most scientifically productive ground-based observatories, with almost 300 refereed publications a year.

caption: Laser guide star beam sweeping across the sky, Paranal Observatory, Chile
story: A powerful laser beam from ESO's Very Large Telescope fans out across the night sky over the Atacama Desert in this image by Julien Girard. The fan comes from the Earth's rotation during the 30-minute exposure and the laser moving to follow it. The same motion stretches the stars into curved trails, which shows their slightly different colours.

The beam makes sodium atoms 90 kilometres up glow, creating an artificial star. Measuring it lets astronomers correct for the atmosphere's blurring, a technique called adaptive optics. Bright natural stars can also serve, but a laser guide star can be placed wherever it is needed, so the technique works across more of the sky.

Below stand the big enclosures of all four 8.2-metre Unit Telescopes, with the smaller VLT Survey Telescope behind. Moving enclosures appear blurred, and faint streaks of light were left by people walking across the platform.
explore: Girard is an ESO astronomer who works at the VLT. That night he was helping with observations on the Unit Telescope furthest to the right, so he set his camera on a fixed tripod before heading back to the control building.
He shared the picture through the Your ESO Pictures Flickr group, which ESO reviews for its Picture of the Week series.

caption: The Magellanic Clouds above ALMA antennas, Chajnantor plateau, Chile
story: The Large and Small Magellanic Clouds glow brightly above the antennas of ALMA, the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array, in this image by ESO Photo Ambassador Christoph Malin. It is a single still frame from one of his carefully made time-lapse videos of the observatory.

The two Magellanic Clouds are nearby irregular dwarf galaxies, easy to see without any telescope from the southern hemisphere. Both circle our own galaxy, and there are signs that close passes near the Milky Way have pulled both of them badly out of shape.

ALMA stands 5000 metres up, on the Chajnantor Plateau. ESO describes it as the world's most powerful telescope for studying the Universe at millimetre and submillimetre wavelengths, light far beyond what the eye can see. At the time this picture was released, construction was still under way, with a total of 66 high-precision antennas planned for the site.
explore: Europe, North America and East Asia share ALMA, in cooperation with the Republic of Chile. ESO leads construction and operations for Europe, the National Radio Astronomy Observatory for North America, and the National Astronomical Observatory of Japan for East Asia.

caption: Laser beams and star trails above the Very Large Telescope, Paranal Observatory, Chile
story: Long arcs of starlight curve across the sky above ESO's Paranal Observatory in this photograph, taken over several hours. Beams of orange light burst from one of the Unit Telescopes, and a smaller Auxiliary Telescope sits in the foreground on the right.

The Very Large Telescope combines four big Unit Telescopes with four smaller Auxiliary Telescopes that can be moved around. The orange beams come from the Four Laser Guide Star Facility, which sets sodium atoms high in the atmosphere glowing as artificial stars. The twinkling of those artificial stars is measured in real time, and the adaptive optics system uses it to undo the atmosphere's blurring so the telescope can take sharp images.

Each laser delivers 22 watts, roughly 4000 times the legal limit for a laser pointer, and its beam is about 30 centimetres wide. The beams point in opposite directions only because, during the hours-long exposure, the telescope moved to observe different targets.
explore: ESO describes the VLT as one of the most advanced optical telescopes in the world.

caption: The Milky Way behind Unit Telescope 4, Paranal Observatory, Chile
story: As the Sun sets over ESO's Paranal Observatory, the Milky Way emerges in fine detail behind Unit Telescope 4, known as Yepun. Paranal is home to the Very Large Telescope, the flagship facility of European ground-based astronomy.
To the naked eye, the Milky Way looks like a cloudy haze across the sky. In reality it is made of 100–400 billion individual stars spread along its 100 000 light-year length.

Yepun is the word for Venus in the language of the Mapuche, the indigenous people of southern Chile. It belongs to a set of four 8.2-metre telescopes that can be combined to act as one giant telescope, letting astronomers see details up to 16 times finer than any single telescope could. Working together, the VLT has opened a new age of discovery, with several notable scientific firsts, among them following single stars as they orbit the supermassive black hole at our galaxy's centre.
explore: ESO Photo Ambassador John Colosimo took the picture and shared it through the Your ESO Pictures Flickr group, which ESO regularly reviews to choose images for its Picture of the Week series and gallery.

caption: Laser guide stars and the Milky Way above Unit Telescope 4, Paranal Observatory, Chile
story: Four powerful laser beams leave Unit Telescope 4, or Yepun, at ESO's Very Large Telescope in Chile's Atacama Desert. Behind them, the familiar band of the Milky Way stretches across the sky, almost appearing to follow the beams, and a faint green wash of airglow tints the sky.

The beams form the VLT's 4 Laser Guide Star Facility, part of a technology called adaptive optics. Turbulence in the atmosphere makes stars twinkle and blur. To undo that, a deformable mirror reshapes itself as often as 1000 times a second, guided by the turbulence astronomers measure by watching a bright star in the field of view.

When no suitable star is available, they make one. The lasers shine at a very particular orange-yellow colour, a wavelength of 589 nm, which excites sodium atoms about 90 km up so they glow like a star. Airglow is light given off naturally by atoms and molecules in the atmosphere, visible only where skies are free of light pollution.

caption: The Carina Nebula and star clusters above an ALMA antenna, Chajnantor plateau, Chile
story: Three deep-sky objects seem to shine just in front of the dish of an ALMA antenna in this single-exposure image, taken during the ESO Ultra HD Expedition. The most prominent is the reddish Carina Nebula. To its upper right is the star cluster NGC 3532, and to its upper left the cluster IC 2602.

The Carina Nebula is a large cloud of gas, mostly hydrogen, where stars have recently formed. Massive, short-lived blue stars born inside it pour out ultraviolet radiation that ionises the gas, making hydrogen glow its characteristic red. In time, supernovae and strong stellar winds will scatter the gas, leaving one or more star clusters behind, much like the two nearby.
The French astronomer Nicolas Louis de Lacaille was the first to catalogue all three, which lie in Carina, the Keel. Though they look close together in the sky, their distances differ greatly.
explore: IC 2602 is under 500 light-years away and NGC 3532 around 1300 light-years away, while the Carina Nebula is thought to be up to 10 000 light-years distant.

caption: The Milky Way over La Silla Observatory, Chile
story: The Milky Way rises above ESO's La Silla Observatory, its bright band dotted with red star-forming regions and woven with dark filaments of dust. Two of the site's telescopes are in view, the 1-metre Schmidt telescope on the left and the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope on the right. Just above the 2.2-metre, towards the centre-right, is the Large Magellanic Cloud, a neighbouring dwarf galaxy, and a pink and green glow of airglow hangs just over the horizon.

Every star in the sky belongs to our galaxy, but only this streak is called the Milky Way. The reason is the galaxy's shape, like a giant pancake with a bright central bulge, and nearly all its stars, gas and dust lie in a thin disc. The Solar System sits on one spiral arm, roughly two-thirds of the way out from the centre. The bright band is our view along that disc, looking in towards the crowded centre.
explore: Airglow comes from excited atoms high in the Earth's upper atmosphere.

caption: The BlackGEM telescopes under the Milky Way, La Silla Observatory, Chile
story: The Milky Way sparkles above BlackGEM, the newest addition to ESO's La Silla Observatory in Chile's Atacama Desert, its band crowded with stars and veiled by dark dust and glowing gas. A haze of ruby red and emerald green lights the scene. The rightmost pillar is empty here, but a third dome has since been installed on it.

BlackGEM is an array of optical telescopes built to find the sources of gravitational waves using visible light. Collisions of black holes and neutron stars send ripples through spacetime, which detectors such as Virgo and LIGO can pick up. BlackGEM then tries to pinpoint where they happened by searching the sky for short-lived events, such as sources of light that appear or vanish within a single night. Larger telescopes like ESO's Very Large Telescope can then follow up in more detail.
The red and green haze is airglow, produced mainly by chemical reactions between atoms high in the atmosphere.
explore: BlackGEM works hand in hand with gravitational-wave observatories including EGO-Virgo and LIGO.

caption: Orion and the Milky Way above the VLT Survey Telescope, Paranal Observatory, Chile
story: The soft glow of the Milky Way pours like a waterfall over the VLT Survey Telescope at ESO's Paranal Observatory. Just outside the galaxy's band, a few stars stand out. The bright reddish one is Betelgeuse and the fainter white star to its left is Bellatrix, the two shoulders of Orion the Hunter. Above them, three stars in a straight line form Orion's belt, and nearby is the purple-tinged glow of the Orion Nebula.

Betelgeuse, a red supergiant some 640 light-years off, is thought to be close to exploding as a supernova. The Orion Nebula looks like a fuzzy patch to the naked eye, but binoculars or a telescope show a nebula where huge amounts of star formation are taking place.

At 2635 metres above sea level, the VST enjoys exceptionally clear skies. It is the largest telescope in the world devoted to surveying the sky in visible light, and its work ranges from finding remote Solar System bodies to studying our galaxy's structure.
explore: The VST also searches for exoplanet transits, the slight dimming when a planet crosses in front of its star, and contributes to studies of how our galaxy has evolved.

caption: Star trails over Cerro Armazones, Chile
story: At first sight this picture could be ripples spreading from a stone dropped into a lake. In fact, the long bright stripes are star trails over Cerro Armazones, a peak 3046 metres above sea level in the central Atacama Desert, in the Chilean Andes. Every stripe traces one star's journey across the night.

The stars' motion is too slow for the naked eye to notice, but leaving a camera's shutter open reveals it. Exposures as short as 15 minutes are enough. The photographer combined many shorter exposures into the final picture, and a very wide-angle lens takes in the celestial pole on the right and the celestial equator just over the short tower.

The sheer number of trails shows how good the sky at Armazones is. The air is extremely clear and, thanks to the remote mountaintop, there is no light pollution. That is one reason the mountain was chosen as the future home of the European Extremely Large Telescope.
explore: ESO describes the planned telescope as set to become the world's biggest eye on the sky.

understand.eye: The eye sees stars as fixed points. Only long exposure time, here built up from many shorter exposures, turns their slow motion into these rippling trails.

caption: The Milky Way above the Extremely Large Telescope construction site, Cerro Armazones, Chile
story: Countless stars, along with the Milky Way's hazy band, shine clearly above the construction site of the Extremely Large Telescope on Cerro Armazones in Chile. Seeing the Milky Way this distinctly takes a place with little light pollution, like this mountain, and a night with little or no moonlight.

When it starts operating, the ELT will be 'the world's biggest eye on the sky'. With a 39-metre primary mirror, it will search in optical and near-infrared light for new exoplanets, especially Earth-like planets orbiting other stars. It will also carry out a kind of 'stellar archaeology', tackling basic questions about how planets, the first stars, early galaxies and black holes form and evolve.

Perhaps its most exciting goal is to measure directly how quickly the Universe's expansion is speeding up. Astronomers have known for decades that galaxies are moving apart, and now think the expansion is accelerating. Measuring that directly would greatly deepen our understanding of the Universe.
explore: ESO lists this image as part of its Cosmic Gems programme, an outreach initiative that uses telescope time unsuitable for science to make images for education and public outreach.

caption: The Coalsack Nebula above an Auxiliary Telescope, Paranal Observatory, Chile
story: A person's silhouette stands out against one of the Auxiliary Telescopes at ESO's Paranal Observatory in Chile's Atacama Desert, while the Coalsack Nebula appears as a dark smudge at the centre of the starry sky.

The telescope is one of four 1.8-metre Auxiliary Telescopes belonging to ESO's Very Large Telescope, alongside four giant 8.2-metre Unit Telescopes. Depending on each project's needs, the Auxiliary Telescopes can be moved along tracks to up to 30 observing positions. Working together as the VLT Interferometer, they combine the light they gather, letting researchers see the cosmos in great detail.

Of all the dark nebulae in the sky, the Coalsack is the most prominent. It is rich in dust, which absorbs and scatters most of the starlight behind it, so it appears as a dark smudge in the sky. Infrared light, however, passes through dust almost unhindered, so the hidden stars can be seen at those wavelengths. Dark clouds like this stand out more from the southern hemisphere than from the north.
explore: Many cultures see shapes in these dark clouds. The Mapuche people of Chile call the Coalsack pozoko, meaning 'water well'.

caption: The Southern Cross and Alpha and Beta Centauri over La Silla Observatory, Chile
story: The Southern Cross is easy to spot in the dark sky over ESO's La Silla Observatory, just right of the Danish 1.54-metre telescope's dome. Towards the lower right sparkle two stars, Alpha Centauri on the right and Beta Centauri on the left. Alpha Centauri, a multiple star, is the closest star system to Earth.

Its third member, Proxima Centauri, is too faint to see with the naked eye but is a little closer than the bright pair, just 4.2 light-years away, making it our nearest neighbour. Past observations offered faint hints that a small companion circles this red dwarf.

A campaign called the Pale Red Dot, which began in January 2016, set out to search more sensitively for the tiny wobbles in Proxima's motion that could reveal an Earth-like planet. The main tool was HARPS, the High Accuracy Radial velocity Planet Searcher on ESO's 3.6-metre telescope at La Silla.
explore: HARPS measurements were complemented by the Las Cumbres Observatory Global Telescope Network and the BOOTES system. The campaign also invited the public to follow the observations as they came in, with blog posts by astronomers, engineers and science writers on planet-hunting and the lives of stars.
